Our solution algorithm is approximate and runs in linear time for each iteration, allowing it to be much faster than exact algorithms that can run in exponential time (Section 5 describes the approximation and algorithm).

Named Entity Recognition (NER) involves detecting and classifying named entities mentioned in unstructured text into predefined categories. Traditionally, the task of NER involved identifying entities within fewer clearly-defined categories such as PERSON, ORGANIZATION, LOCATION, and EMAIL. However, as natural language processing becomes increasingly important in various applications such as question answering, information extraction, and semantic web, the need for a more fine-grained semantic classification system has become apparent. The ability to classify named entities into more specific and detailed categories can significantly enhance the performance and utility of NLP applications. This paper addresses the challenge of fine-grained semantic class induction, a task aimed at automatically determining which of a larger set of predefined, fine-grained semantic classes a given noun phrase belongs to. This problem is particularly prevalent and significant in applications where semantic class information needs to support a wide range of natural language processing tasks. The paper proposes two main techniques to improve the standard approach to fine-grained semantic class induction: hierarchical classification and collective classification.   Hierarchical Classification:   In a hierarchical classification approach, each fine-grained semantic class is not considered independent but rather is organized in a hierarchy. For instance, within the category of "POLITICAL POSITION," there might be subcategories such as "President," "Senator," "Governor," and so forth. A hierarchical classifier learns to rank both at the top-level (e.g., POLITICAL POSITION) and sub-levels (e.g., President, Senator). This approach allows for more nuanced predictions and leverages the natural hierarchical structure in the semantic classes.   Collective Classification:   Collective classification, also known as multi-instance learning, treats a set of entities together as one instance. For example, all noun phrases in a document (or a larger document collection) might be treated as an "instance." This approach is particularly effective in situations where determining the fine-grained semantic class for one entity can benefit from knowing the contextual information and classes of neighboring entities. Collective classification can thus make more accurate predictions by aggregating evidence from multiple entities in the context. The paper argues that these methods, either individually or in combination, can significantly enhance the performance of traditional supervised learning approaches to fine-grained semantic class induction. The hypothesis is that hierarchical classification can capture the nested structure of semantic concepts, while collective classification can compensate for the sparse and imbalanced data often encountered in fine-grained classification tasks by leveraging aggregative evidence from multiple instances.

Topdown parsing works well particularly for predicting well-formed sentences but can exhibit a range of oddball behavior. However, many top-down parsers do not produce fully connected trees for every alternative parse – they typically output at most just the best single parse, or only partially connected parses. This is not like how humans process sentences – among semanticists and cognitive psychologists there is a broad consensus that we parse sentences "incrementally", that is to say that we have a partly progressed parse structure which is continually refined and expanded during the process of reading. Ron Kaplan, for example, in a study using eye-tracking techniques (Kaplan & Friederici, 2009), showed that readers gain information incrementally as they read. Now Forbs (2014) and Roark (2001) demonstrated different ways to create top-down parsers that maintain a finite set of competing fully connected parse trees. However in all cases the acquisition and maintenance of several trees during the parsing process requires a very substantial amount of computation or carefully careful inference over very large numbers of features. In this paper, I describe an algorithm for top-down parsing that proceeds left-to-right character by character but which does maintain between one and a few full trees at all times. Named Entity Recognition (NER) involves detecting and classifying named entities mentioned in unstructured text into predefined categories. Bilingual Named Entity (NE) recognition and alignment are related tasks that require identifying and relating the corresponding named entities in two different languages. The two main tasks involved in bilingual NE recognition and alignment are: (1) named entity recognition in one language, and (2) cross-lingual named entity alignment between the two languages. The ultimate goal of bilingual NE recognition and alignment is to establish the correspondence between named entities of two languages as accurately and completely as possible. Recognizing NEs from text data extracted from an individual language can be a relatively simple task due to the knowledge and lexical resources available for those languages. However, when there is a need to map such NEs into another language, additional challenges arise from semantic differences, different word usage and expressions, even for straightforward entities like proper nouns. These differences can be particularly significant in the recognition of entities like person names, organization names, or location names. Furthermore, certain entity types such as dates, numbers, or percentages may have different representations across languages, which can complicate the alignment process. The challenge of bilingual NE recognition and alignment becomes even more pronounced when dealing with implicit named entities or those relying on contexts or cultural knowledge. For instance, a given entity like "30th of November" might be explicitly mentioned as "30 Nov." in English and "30月11日" in Chinese. However, if the English text only uses the number "30" or the date in the form "November 30th", without explicitly mentioning the day, the task becomes more complex as one needs to infer or recognize the named entity in both languages, possibly by considering additional context or understanding of the culturally specific ways of expressing dates. Additionally, when two languages have different writing systems or scripts (e.g., Chinese and English), the recognition of named entities requires adaptation and often the use of additional resources, such as transliteration or tokenization rules tailored for each language. The lack of one-to-one correspondences between NE types across languages adds another layer of complexity. What counts as a "person name" or "location" can have different granularity or characteristics in different languages and cultures, and these differences need to be understood and accounted for in the alignment process. To address these complexities, an integrated model for bilingual named entity recognition and alignment can be proposed.

However, traditional word representation methods based on distributional semantics, such as those utilized by Word2Vec and GloVe (Pennington et al., 2014), rely solely on co-occurrence information and consequently do not inherently account for the emotional dimensions of words. This limitation is particularly problematic for tasks that require an understanding of emotional content in text. Sentiment analysis, emotion classification, and affect-based natural language generation are all examples of applications where word representations need to capture the emotional connotations of words. For instance, words like "happy" and "sad", while having distinct emotional meanings, might be used in similar contexts and thus could end up being represented closely in traditional word embedding spaces. Conversely, it may be desirable to model words with similar emotional meanings as being more closely related, such as "joyful" and "glad", irrespective of their exact contextual usage. In this paper, we propose an approach to enriching word representations with information about emotional similarity. We introduce emotion-enriched word representations that project emotionally similar words into neighboring spaces and emotionally distinct words far apart. Our method is designed to create embeddings that capture not only linguistic but also affective properties of words, making them significantly more appropriate for emotion-related tasks. The proposed method introduces a new challenge: how to determine emotional similarity without relying on a labeled corpus. To overcome this, we leverage distant supervision from publicly available socio-linguistic resources and the distributional properties of words that can be learned from unannotated textual data. Specifically, we utilize recurrent neural networks (RNNs) to learn emotion-related contexts for words and subsequently adjust traditional embeddings based on these learned contexts. The proposed method can be summarized as follows: 1. Distant Supervision: Harvesting emotion information from socio-linguistic resources and web-based lexica to generate a large, though partially noisy, corpus of text documents labeled for emotional connotation. 2. Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) Context Modeling: Using RNNs to capture contextual information indicative of word emotional meaning. This step involves training an RNN to predict whether a word is likely to appear in a context that evokes either high or low levels of a given emotion (e.g., happiness).

Words are considered similar if they tend to appear in corresponding contexts, which can be contextually defined and often corresponds to semantic and sometimes syntactic similarity (Silver et al., 2016) . There are several ways to estimate word similarity. The word embeddings (Mikolov et al., 2013a, 2013b) , which are word representations in a low-dimensional vector space, have been widely adopted in various NLP tasks and often used as features for measuring similarity. Sentence embedding (Kiros et al., 2015; Conneau et al., 2017; Logeswaran & Lee, 2018) is another approach which embeds a paragraph or sentence into a vector for capturing longer context. Another very effective way, originally proposed by Li and Jurafsky (2011) and further explored in Deerwester et al. (1990) , is the use of a context vector, which is computed from the co-occurrences of the target word in the training corpus. This method works well and is easy to compute given the need to preprocess the corpus only at the beginning and store it to the memory, followed by an efficient computation of the similarity for every word pair (Peñas & Rodrigo, 2011) . However, it has the drawback of being inapplicable as a streaming algorithm because it requires full memory access, and all contexts must be processed and stored before any similarity can be calculated. The ideal NLP pipeline should be able to handle real-time input, treating the incoming stream of textual data as continuous and potentially unbounded (Arasu & Vassilvitskii, 2000) . This allows real-time information processing, adapting to new topics or world events as they emerge, without having to explicitly retrain on large static datasets. Streaming word similarities are also highly beneficial in situations where memory is a constrained resource, such as in mobile applications or edge AI where data can be processed locally with limited memory capabilities (Vanwinge & Rodrigues, 2016) . Rapidly assessing word similarities in streaming text without calculating them from scratch or relying heavily on precomputed embeddings has significant practical implications. In this paper, we present a novel streaming algorithm for estimating word similarities based on co-occurrence counts and second-order co-occurrences. Our approach is innovative because it inherently works with streams (online algorithm) by summarizing co-occurrence counts into buffers per word, thus reducing the computational complexity and memory requirements by orders of magnitude compared to the traditional context vector approach while still capturing semantic similarities effectively.

These models, which incorporate comprehensive statistical and linguistic knowledge, have achieved remarkable progress in bridging gaps between languages (Devlin et al., 2017). However, most of these advancements are based on the translation of text across different languages and, as such, do not leverage the structure inherently present in the source text, such as syntax or semantic relations, unless explicitly engineered into the model structure (Luong et al., 2015). This structural information would not only allow for knowledge transfer across languages but could also improve the generation of the target texts by ensuring adherence to the syntactic and semantic structure of the language. Tree-structured models are one way to incorporate and translate this information. Tree-to-string models (TST), in essence, represent a translation step where the source sentence is first parsed into a syntactic structure and then this tree is translated into the target language. TST models can be further subdivided into two categories: those that only replace subtrees (substitution-based models) and those that can also add new structure or modify existing structure (adjunction-based models). The problem of string-to-tree models, where a given string is parsed into a tree structure, has been well studied in different settings (Chen and Manning, 2014;Klein and Manning, 2003). For string-to-tree models, it is common to model the parsing process using techniques such as dynamic programming (DP) (Eisner, 1996), as in shift-reduce parsers, or through the use of neural networks for more complex structures (Dyer et al., 2014). However, the reverse process, from tree to string, is less well understood and has garnered less attention in the literature, particularly when considering the incorporation of adjoinments. This might be due to the inherent complexity of predicting or generating new side of the tree without a clear structure or template to follow. This paper proposes an extension to conventional tree-to-string translation to incorporate adjunctions explicitly through the use of synchronous Tree-Adjoining Grammars (TAGs). TAGs are a formal language theory framework that can naturally model structures through substitution (insertion of a subtree into a leaf node) and adjunction (insertion of a new node or subtree into the tree by adjoining structure from a so-called adjunct). The added value of TAG-based translation is the ability to generate or reconstruct the target sentence while adhering to the adjoinment rules which can encode richer linguistic structures and relations.

Semantic role labeling (SRL) is a fundamental task in natural language processing aimed at identifying predicate-argument structures in text. Given a predicate, the task is to identify the arguments and their respective roles in relation to the predicate. SRL is crucial because it provides semantic information that can be used for a wide range of NLP tasks, including machine translation, question answering, and information extraction. Early work in SRL primarily relied on hand-crafted rules and features derived from shallow parsing. However, in recent years, there has been a significant shift towards deep learning methods. These methods, typically rooted in recurrent neural networks, learn features directly from raw text and have shown impressive performance in various NLP tasks, including SRL. This performance surge has in some places suggested that syntactic information—often derived from specialized linguistic parsers—might be less crucial than expected for SRL. Some recent models have even achieved top performance without explicitly using syntactic analysis, raising the question of the importance of syntactic information in modern neural SRL models. However, this perspective overlooks the potential synergies that could arise from incorporating or even inferring syntactic information in a neural learning framework. Syntactic structures encode valuable semantic information that can aid in disambiguating the roles of arguments. For instance, understanding the grammatical structure of a sentence can help distinguish the subject of the verb from its object, or to identify coreference chains. The neglect of syntactic information could result in models that are over-eager to label arguments based on superficial lexical co-occurrence, without fully considering the semantic roles in context. Moreover, for languages with syntactically rich structures, syntactic features might not only improve performance but also help in model generalization. For example, languages with complex case systems (like those found in Russian or Hindi) or contextual markers (common in East Asian languages), could benefit significantly from structured syntactic information in the SRL process. Therefore, this paper seeks to investigate the role of syntactic information in achieving state-of-the-art performance on SRL tasks. Specifically, we will explore whether and how deep learning models can benefit quantitatively from explicitly incorporating or implicitly inferring syntactic information. Our work takes inspiration from existing literature that has shown the potential benefits of combining deep learning approaches with more structured linguistic information for tasks like parsing (Andor et al., 2016;Dozat and Manning, 2016) or dependency syntax (Martins et al., 2017).

Comments, on the other hand, allow readers to voice their own views directly related to or in response to the original post. While they offer a unique opportunity to study knowledge claims and opinions, comments, especially on political blog posts, can frequently become subject to disruptive verbal attacks, irrelevant diatribes, or repetitive posts. Sentiment analysis (Hutto and Gilbert, 2014;Thelwall, 2010) and content analysis (Ledford and D’Ignazio, 2013) have traditionally targeted sentiment and opinion content in user-generated text, such as comments and user reviews. Recent extensions have introduced topic models (Blei et al., 2003;Wallach et al., 2009) to these domains For instance, Weinshall et al. (2010) found distinct topic models for comments expressing support and criticism. However, predicting who would comment on a given post has received little attention. Stated as a prediction task, it is also plausible that the content variables such as extent to which the post resonates (e.g., whether the post is focused on a topic of interest) or stirs emotions (e.g., whether the post is polarizing) can influence the propensity of a user to leave a comment and may reveal hidden patterns in the political discourse community. In this work, we investigate user behavior in response to different political blog content using topic models to highlight similarities and differences between blog posts and their associated comments. We extend LDA to jointly model the blog post contents and a probabilistic latent variable representation of the community of commenters. We further innovate to allocate uncertainty over commenters' latent factors, and explore its potential for confronting disruptions such as spamming or sensationalist changing the topics. With these models, we define a novel predictive task to forecast which users out of a large user base are likely to comment on any given post. On a widely used dataset of political blog posts and associated comments, we show that topic information about the post helps predict commenter identity, and that models accounting for user variability are more effective.

TSFG is capable of capturing both the textual cues embedded in a user's messages/posts, such as gender indicative language, and the latent "same-interest" structure in social networks. This combined representation enables our method to effectively exploit both sources of evidence to improve gender classification accuracy. We explore various instantiations of the proposed method in different network settings and contexts to derive general conclusions about the importance of textual features versus "same-interest" links and highlight conditions under which the combined approach provides the most robust performance. Social media platforms, such as Twitter, have become a fundamental source of real-time first-hand information about breaking news events. These platforms have also been involved in several incidences where the noise from fake or manipulated news stories has spread rapidly and had various sociopolitical consequences. To mitigate these issues, scholars have proposed and developed various methods, from content-based strategies to leverage questions or status updates from cross-event distributions (Silberholz et al., 2015;Pang and Lee, 2004;Procter et al., 2013), to more complex network-based strategies that use co-occurrences and structural information in networks (Varol et al., 2017;Shao et al., 2017;Varol and Gore, 2018). Sentiment analysis (a.k.a. opinion mining or semantic orientation analysis) has been shown to be useful in identifying the overall "tone" of news reports/tweets related to specific events (Trivedi and Liu, 2010;John et al., 2015;Johansson et al., 2015). However, in general, it is still far from sophisticated enough to accommodate the diverse or even contradictory sentiments that are often found in a given event. One major challenge in sentiment analysis is how accurately to quantify different levels of sentiment with shallow text models that may often assumed binary while the underlying reality can be much more nuanced. For instance, people expressing opinions about complex, long-lasting events often exhibit different levels of sentiment (e.g., from very positive to very negative). To address this issue, we conducted an intensive study on developing deep learning-based models that: i) are specifically designed to deal with the challenges in capturing varied contexts and sentiments in early event reports through a model that learns effective word embeddings and uses them to contextualize sentiment scores; and ii) effectively leverage contextual information and sentiment signals to identify authentic news reports and detect or mitigate the spread of fake news or less credible content in ongoing events. Our approach utilizes a combination of deep learning techniques, particularly leveraging the Sequence-to-Sequence (Seq2Seq) model architecture and contextualized word embeddings, to capture the dynamic and varied sentiment expressions in real-time event feeds. Specifically, we extend the standard Seq2Seq model by incorporating two novel advanced features – a) a deep word embedding model that learns representations of words from large text corpora but also, unlike Word2Vec or GloVe, remains fine-tuned on the specific contexts (news-related posts, in this case) to be more effective for sentiment analysis in dynamic events; and b) an attention-based technique that allows the model to focus on specific parts of the input text that are relevant for the sentiment determination task.

Training NLP systems can be thought of as optimize a system for achieving a minimum error criterion. Traditionally, this optimization is performed using an error rate estimation function that measures how well the system performs on a set of example sentences, and a search algorithm that adjusts the model parameters in order to minimize the empirical error, as defined by this function. This optimization step is crucial to the performance of machine translation (MT) and speech recognition, among many other NLP tasks (Och, 2003;Sennrich et al., 2010). In practice, for most tasks, the optimization keeps changing model parameters alongside a set of N-best hypotheses for a training set, while iterating, until the optimization algorithm cannot improve the objective function further. These N-best lists are often used for training because directly optimizing over Sentence A (a structured derived directly from Sentence B) via maximizing a weighted sum of word bigrams can be misleading even if each of the individual weights properly reflects individual components of expected loss (e.g., the bigram “put/through” may sometimes carry a positive weight even if in a given context it would be better to have “put through” in one word). Thus, for achieving the best end-to-end model or even for tuning scoring components that are used inside this context, working with N-best lists remains essential but is not optimal. These traditional methods are often based on a form of stochastic gradient descent on the error estimate. However, in practice, the acquisition and use of these estimates to update parameters are often far from the theory. In reality, estimates are often noisy, and the inference for MT (or ASSISTANT, VISUAL RECOGNITION in practice) outputs can be more complex than a single sentence. Properly optimizing parameter and model choices through a minimum-error-error-rate doesn’t come without its challenges. Many error rate estimates for NLP tasks, such as BLEU (Papineni et al., 2002) for MT or word error rate (WER) in speech recognition, are designed to evaluate the matched output against a reference. They are not designed to guide a learning or search procedure. For classic machine learning, one might confront non-convexities in loss functions, but in language, the N-best lists add another layer of non-convexity because choices interact with each other – choosing option A for decision B can in complex ways influence option C and D in later decisions.

Social media platforms, especially Twitter, represent a valuable source for any analysis of real-world events. The content of Twitter can be used to monitor ongoing situations around the globe and provide insights about unfolding narratives. One key challenge in the analysis of Twitter content is to be able to distill its essence into a set of key phrases (keyphrases) – descriptive phrase questions or statements that reflect what conversations are about and convey the gist and the topic of the content at hand (Strube and Mayfield, 2009). In the absence of appropriate word representations (e.g., for non-English languages) and due to the brevity and informality of many tweets, standard natural language processing techniques, such as dependency parsing (Nivre, 2007) or part-of-speech tagging (Hulden, 2009), may not be as effective as in longer, more structured texts. The task of identifying keyphrases has been actively studied in the context of web search, document summarization, and information retrieval (Tellex and Katz, 2007;Smith et al., 2006;Strube and Mayfield, 2009). In contrast to these contexts, where documents often are long and sequentially structured, tweets are short and mostly sequenced in a non-sequential fashion. These distinctive characteristics of Twitter data make traditional keyphrase extraction methods less effective. This paper presents a novel keyphrase extraction method that is specifically designed to handle the distinct features of Twitter data. We propose an approach that carefully builds on topical relevance and linguistic relevance to generate topical keyphrases as an efficient way to summarize Twitter content. Our approach, termed Topical Keyphrase Extraction from Twitter (ToKeT), is driven by the observation that topical keyphrases likely carry socio-linguistic ties to the colloquial and topical nature that Twitter users exhibit. The ToKeT framework includes two main design components: 1) A context-sensitive topical PageRank method for keyword ranking: This component leverages the latent, topical structure inherent in Twitter. Instead of traditional PageRank applied to a graph of web pages, we create a graph where nodes are words, edges are co-occurrences of words in a tweet, and edge weights are determined using our context-sensitive topical PageRank algorithm. This algorithm assigns a score to each word based on how likely it is to indicate a topic and how informative it is given the co-occurrence patterns with other words. 2) A probabilistic scoring function for keyphrase ranking that considers relevance and interestingness: After obtaining the topical PageRank scores for each word, we generate candidate keyphrases by considering all possible sequences of two or three scored words found co-occurring in the same tweet.

Through CDS, young children are exposed to a vast array of linguistic structures that they must then learn and incorporate into their developing linguistic systems. This includes word meaning (vocabulary learning), word form (phonological and morphological segmentation), and word order (syntactic structure knowledge). One essential question in language acquisition research concerns how these different levels of linguistic structure are learned simultaneously, often by children with very little prior language knowledge. Is learning one level (e.g., vocabulary) necessary for learning another (e.g., syntax), or can these levels be acquired in a self-contained manner? An important theoretical perspective holds that certain levels of linguistic structure, such as syntax and morphology, are not isolated systems, but rather interact in meaningful ways during learning (Paradis, 2005;Hudson Kam and Newport, 2005;Weirich, 2020). For this reason, it is plausible that simultaneously learning both morphology and syntax could lead to better overall understanding and faster learning of each system than if the two levels were learned in sequence. This perspective has motivated research into computational models that learn to segment words into morphemes while simultaneously identifying the syntactic category of words or phrases (e.g., noun, verb, etc.). However, there is still little consensus on the nature and extent of interaction between learning at different linguistic levels, and the benefits and challenges of joint learning. Part of the reason for this lack of consensus is that previous computational models have mostly focused on learning only one level of structure at a time, and the few existing cross-level models (e.g., Yang et al., 2012;Li and Lewis, 2015;Piper et al., 2017) were applied to tasks without explicit concurrent learning goals or were presented mainly as proof-of-concept approaches with limited empirical validation across diverse language environments. In changing the focus to learning both morphology and syntax together, one can address a core theoretical question while also contributing to the development of more flexible and generalizable computational models of language acquisition. The challenge is, however, substantial: such models require the capacity for information sharing across tasks (morphological segmentations and syntactic categorization), which can be difficult to engineer given the almost entirely distinct nature of the linguistic evidence and the goals of these tasks.

Training methods for coreference resolution can be broadly categorized into two types: strict (or binary) classification and mention-pair scoring. In the first category, the task is assumed to be a two-class classification problem (Coreference or Not-coreference), where individual mentions are labeled with one of these two labels. In the second category, a score (positive or negative depending on the kind of metric used) is given to each mention-pair as an indication of their "likelihood" to be coreferent. There is of course, a third option where mentions are assigned scores based on how likely they are to refer to an antecedent (Chen and Manning, 2014). This paper primarily focuses on the second category. Strict classification can lead to inaccurate training for the coreference task due to the nature of the task. Sentences that have multiple coreferences will result in multiple Not-coreference labels, even if a strict classifier performs well on the "Two-mentions-does-not-need-to-be-coreference-but-has-to-be-Coreference-or-Not-Coreference" instances. Furthermore, proper estimation of the evaluation metric (could be F1, B-CUBED (Baeza-Yates and Ribeiro-Neto, 1996), or MUC Forth (MUC4) (Chinchor, 1993)) is often sacrificed for training accuracy. This paper proposes a new metric-based training approach that benefits from label smoothing in learning; the approach significantly improves evaluation metric scores over the coreference resolution training. A key insight in this approach is using distinctively worse (worst possible) scores as "not-coreference" instances to encourage the model to predict in accordance with the evaluation metric. One could argue that the "wrong" instances are already penalized and "proper" model optimization could be approached with real values (1 and 0 for "coreference" and "not-coreference" respectively). However, our experiments with label smoothing demonstrate otherwise (Xie et al., 2016;Reed et al., 2015). The base model used in our experiments is based on dependency parsing. However, this new training method can be applied to any coreference framework and will be beneficial as it promotes a more direct optimization towards the evaluation metric. This is especially useful in situations where the coreferential mentions span sentences (or some are missing in the training/prediction set and others in the evaluation set, as seen in the MUC corpora). Unlike previous works that use some form of score thresholding after training (Raghunathan et al., 2010;Raghunathan and Jha, 2008; 2010), our approach directly optimizes the evaluation metric score during training.

Automatic construction of news overview articles from multiple news stories or articles is an important task, especially with the increase of today's online news volume. An overview article could summarize a series of unfolding news events, provide comprehensive information and insights, and serve as a comprehensive entry point to the story for readers. A particular challenge in this task, however, is that the input questions are not given: one must instead discover and represent the key aspects and relations between the news articles, and represent them in a coherent text format. In this paper, we report our recent work on automatic news overview text generation. Unlike previous work focused on document summarization given a set of input documents (e.g., Radev et al., 2004; Sarker and Tonella, 2007; Takeuchi et al., 2015), we aim to construct a coherent article among semantic entities (i.e., events, locations, persons, organizations, etc.) discovered from multiple news articles. Hence, we name this task news synthesis, which shares the spirit with multi-document summarization but differs in its creative and comprehensive text generation. We formulate the task as a pair of entity-based selection and hierarchical text generation. Specifically, for a given set of input news articles or a news cluster, we first segment the main event content from each news story, identify semantic entities and their relations using different levels of entity mentions, recognize the event structure and entity relationships while modeling event causality. After that, the entire event structure and semantic entities are used as the building blocks to generate an overview article by following a proposed hierarchical text generation framework (Peñas et al., 2011). Instead of using summarization methods directly on text in batches, as in previous approaches, our key insight is the benefits of a structural decomposition and synthesis from "below" (from events and entities). Our approach is compared with typical multi-document summarization methods on the Wikinews dataset and achieves the best performance on both automatic evaluation and manual evaluation. We provide the source code and experimental results of our evaluation at: https://github.com/yourusername/newssynthesis. The rest of the paper is organized as follows. We first explicitly define the news synthesis task in Section 2 . Next, we describe the technical details of the entire pipeline for the proposed news synthesis approach, including entity-based segmentation, salient entity extraction, event structure recognition, and hierarchical text generation for summary article in Section 3 . Section 4 presents experimental evaluation and comparison against baseline methods.

Automated Text Scoring (ATS) is seen as an effective means to provide cost-effective solutions for assessments. These automated systems are particularly valuable in education, where they can be used to grade student essays or other writing tasks, saving time for human assessors and enabling faster feedback to students. ATS systems can also be used in other contexts – for instance, in evaluating the coherence and relevance of job applications or in monitoring and assessing the quality of customer support responses in a business setting. Despite the benefits, constructing an ATS system remains a challenging task. The most influential factor in determining the success of these systems is how well they can capture the nuances of human judgment. Human knowledge and understanding are usually encoded into the system through handcrafted feature engineering, where domain experts identify and design features that are predictive of performance in a certain context. Handcrafting features is a labor-intensive and time-consuming task that requires in-depth knowledge of both language and the domain. These features are typically extracted from the text structure and components such as sentence length, word complexity, and vocabulary diversity. This process, however, suffers from a few inherent limitations. First, handcrafted features might not capture the complex and deep hierarchical structures discernible in texts. Human language is not merely a sequence or a matrix; it is a complex system of meanings, contexts, and subtle symbols. Second, feature engineering is generally not transferable across different tasks or domains because each task requires a tailored set of features. Third, even in domains where the acquisition and design of suitable features is possible, the feature list can become overwhelmingly large, complicating inference for the model while also potentially leading to overfitting. The recent shift towards using deep learning for ATS in natural language processing offers an exciting alternative to labor-intensive feature engineering. Among the many neural network architectures, Long-Short Term Memory (LSTM) networks have shown particular promise in the context of sequential data like text. LSTMs are designed to learn from sequences by retaining information over time or rather over words in the case of text. Their design allows them to capture patterns and dependencies that span over various lengths, a necessity for understanding complex text structures. This paper proposes a novel approach to ATS by using LSTMs to learn word representations in a fully automated framework. While LSTMs are capable of encoding complex temporal structures (for time series data), we extend this concept to capture the sequential dependencies inherent in text.

The performance of these existing approaches is highlighted, demonstrating the potential of AMR for paraphrase detection while also identifying limitations and possible avenues for improvement. We then propose a novel approach that enhances the AMR-based paraphrase detection with latent semantic analysis (LSA). The underlying hypothesis is that paraphrase detection can benefit from the shallow semantic information captured by LSA, while the deeper meaning captured by AMR ensures that detected paraphrases are conceptually consistent. Event types are categorized according to EVENT AGENCY, INVOLVED ENTITIES, CAUSES, EVENT CALENDARS, CONTEXTUAL INFORMATION OF EVENTS, and RELATIONSBETWEEN EVENTS (Uren et al., 2005). Event extraction systems usually process text sequentially and determine the type of event containing a certain trigger, which is the main action of an event (Riedl and Moore, 2006). As a result, trigger identification is the first step and crucial step for successful event extraction. Without the correct identification of triggers, or even without accurate distinction between the true triggers and pseudo triggers, event extraction is certainly problematic (Cohen, 2005; Lin and Pantel, 2001). Currently, the state-of-art in event extraction systems often overfits to training data because the core annotations are often lacking. Issues can arise from the relatively small size of annotated event corpora for Chinese (ACE 2005, 2015 and in-house corpora), which makes it difficult to train general event extraction models (Jin and Lin, 2013). Another issue is the prevalence of pseudo triggers (or false positive triggers) in the input which can easily distract and mislead the event extraction models (Tsai and Chang, 2006; Koenig and More, 2011). While the blurred boundaries between true and false triggers can be problematic, it is even more challenging to explicitly define or characterize triggers for Chinese due to less developed computational framework and linguistic knowledge for Chinese compared to English (Chen et al., 2014). Therefore, a robust event extraction system needs to intelligently identify true triggers and classify these triggers into event types accurately. This requires a method capable of jointly modeling the process of trigger identification and event type determination with real world adaptation to Chinese language characteristics. In this paper, we present a novel joint model for event extraction in Chinese that solves two key problems simultaneously: low quality datasets and vast amounts of pseudo trigger mentions. We incorporate multiple trigger filtering strategies as part of the model to reduce pseudo trigger mentions.

Certainly, here is the study introduction: Machine translation (MT) system combination (MSC) uses multiple MT systems to generate outputs for a source language (SL) sentence. When different MT systems use different word orderings, unrealistic alignment (or hypothesis) can result, and indispensable for improving the performance of MSC is the alignment method that maps output sentences from multiple MT systems to a single context (or canonical) sentence. This alignment process, also called hypothesis alignment (HA), links generated words in different MT outputs to those in the target language (TL) word sequence (or reference set for alignment). The extracted context keeps changing as hypothesis alignment changes. Therefore, the quality of MT system combination depends critically on the quality of the hypothetical word alignments – the misalignment can lead to MMLE (Multiple Main Language Error). Widely used methods for hypothesis alignment include the n-best list alignment among semantic similarity (i.e., semantic relatedness) or word alignment - which we evaluate below, and others. Hence, aligning hypotheses is a key exploration in this paper, with its aim to enhance the process for better performance in MSC. Hypothesis alignment (HA) is similar to statistical sentence alignment (e.g., GIZA++, OSM, or Honalign or FAST) but is different because HA requires more context-aware and less exact matching (e.g., word alignment between SL and TL with shallow structures may not be appropriate for HA while shallow word alignment can still be useful in HA). For HA, the requirement to balance between the plausible context derived from multiple MT systems and the ground truth word sequence for a TL sentence, without over-limitating to exact word alignment, is still an open challenge. Our work begins with evaluating four common word alignment methods for HA, and all are based on word and phrase alignment through a model: GIZA++ (named after Brown 2000 for its use of IBM model 4 and 5, but in practice, GIZA++ handles more complex algorithms), TER (textual entailment ranking), CLA (cross-lingual alignment based on language models), and IHMM (infinite hidden Markov model). Each method outputs word alignments between SL sentences and TL sentences or other SL sentences, but we seek here a word alignment between hypotheses from MT systems. This is where confusion network decoding steps in. Confusion Network (CN) for MSC (see e.g. previously proposed by Chang et al. 2013, but later also developed further for HA see Papineni 2019 and Almahairi 2019) creates a hypothetical alternative sentence that includes all words from the multiple MT systems as its possible words and assigns a probability to each word occurrence position.

Training high-quality Statistical Machine Translation (SMT) models for any pair of languages requires an abundance of high-quality parallel data. However, such data is costly to create and is rarely available for most language pairs. In practice, many unrealized translations (existing parallel sentences) remain untranslated for lack of time and resources (e.g., the European Parliament’s proceedings have only some 1 million sentences translated into a new language out of a corpus of 30 million sentences (Martens, 2010)). Active learning techniques aim at maximizing the utility of resources (e.g., for SMT data collection) by learning to select examples with high information content (e.g., training samples closest to the target solution to improve convergence time (c.f. (Settles, 2010)). The idea of actively selecting sentences that have the highest added value towards improving translation quality was initially proposed by Koehn (2007). They presented a method of choosing sentences to be translated which minimizes the expected loss of the translation quality, known as Active Example Selection (AES). Since their work, several techniques have been introduced for active learning in Statistical Machine Translation (SMT), including greedy ranking methods (Koehn, 2007), a Bayesian approach (Carroll & Das, this volume) and methods based on feature functions (Yamada & Matsumoto, 2006;Weng, 2009;He et al., 2010). These techniques work on sentence or phrase level and do not take into account the additional structure inherent in bilingual parallel texts. The MT task itself also becomes more complex, challenging and interesting in the multilingual scenario: as demonstrated by (Afful & Toral, 2011), improvements in MT over one language pair can ease the task of MT in other language pairs. The EuroParl corpus (Koehn, 2005), for instance, contains sentences translated into multiple languages. As of 2012, there are 88 language pairs with more than 50,000 sentences each and additional 14 language pairs above 40,000 sentences. We focus in this work on multilingual collection scenarios and changing the set of languages present within our multilingual corpus.   An active learning task that selects new input sentences to add to an existing multi-language parallel text set, when attempting to add a new target language. The added language remains within the global multilingual corpus   We set up and investigate the task of adding a new target language to an existing set of parallel texts and use active learning to improve translation accuracy and reduce the number of examples required.   The experiments show that adding a new language to EuroParl and then using active learning to add new sentences results in significant translation quality improvements over a random or greedy sentence selection baseline.

For example, the fields of parsing and semantic role labeling (SRL) involve entirely different challenges and corpora. Parsers aim to disambiguate surface syntax and generate a principled interpretation of a sentence's structure, while SRL systems focus on constructing a more abstract representation of the argument structure, i.e., identifying and labeling the “who does what to whom?” roles. While these tasks are not directly dependent on knowledge from one another, there is clear potential for exploiting mutual benefits – after all, both tasks operate on the same inputs, sentences – and from each other’s knowledge to improve overall system performance. However, among semantic tasks, SRL in particular places little stringent requirement on the form of the sentence’s syntactic parse. As a result, traditional approaches to building joint models have relied heavily on unidirectional flows of information: a parser supplies a syntactic structure which in turn might provide input features to an SRL system. This structure has often served to support the SRL task, but the information never or rarerly flowed in the opposite direction. One argument for allowing and facilitating this bidirectional information flow is rooted in the different levels of "granularity" that each task operates under while still working with the same syntactic/semantic space. A semantic role labeler (SRLer) can serve as an orthographic "filter" capable of identifying structural semantic patterns, potentially making judgments (supported by their own model, learned on their own task data) in areas where the parser is more ambiguous or uncertain. Conversely, SRL features might achieve better generalization and confidence over rare semantic roles when informed by stronger structural hypotheses provided by the parser. While there is the risk that input from one component might introduce noise or excessive complexity for the other, if managed properly, such an interplay could leverage less-explored avenues for improving together the two tasks' precision, efficiency, and generalization capabilities. Several NLP systems indeed allocate intertask feedback explicitly. For instance, some structured learning methods for dependency parsing explicitly consider the projected semantic role annotations when training (Choi and Xing, 2014). However, these structures typically condition only on already identified semantic roles for specific dependency heads during training. Our proposed research goes further, by examining what happens when the SRL system's semantic predictions actively influence the selection of syntactic parses (i.e., leading to parse choice decisions that could improve the quality of the SRL labeling).

Training and evaluation of human language generation systems require strong evaluation metrics. A key question guiding research in this area is how successful various metrics have been at capturing aspects of human quality judgments. Judgment metrics, which are metrics that attempt to mimic human judgment (e.g. BLEU and METEOR for translation and Tatoeba-27 for image captioning), have traditionally been the gold standard for this evaluation and often correlate well with human judgments (Papineni et al., 2002;Vedantam et al., 2010;Kiros et al., 2014). However, due to the inherent difficulties in obtaining reliable human annotations (Li et al., 2016b;c) for tasks such as image captioning and machine translation, relying solely on correlation with human judgments to judge the adequacy of an evaluation metric can be problematic. Additionally, human judgments can be inconsistent even when provided with a benchmark set of human annotations (Fuller and Geva, 1998;Wadler and Doucet, 2002). While human evaluations might provide a general assessment of a system's quality, they often cannot discern whether a major deficiency lies in structure, fluency, or even something as subtle as the correct use of passive voice. One remedy is to develop unit tests for these evaluation metrics. These tests "corrupt" the input data by transforming the system's output in predictable ways and measuring the effect on the metric. Such tests provide a targeted, fine-grained analysis of a metric's strengths and weaknesses, offering insight distinct from that of general human evaluation. In previous work, we conducted metric unit testing for the METEOR and WER metrics on machine translation output by systematically perturbing the data and observing changes in scores. However, that work was limited to machine translation and focused on showing that such testing could be done and the results analyzed. Here we generalize this work by investigating the application of metric unit testing across multiple language generation tasks and the different characteristics that different tasks bring to evaluation. Our goal is a deeper understanding of the utility of metric unit testing as a tool for analyzing and improving metrics, as well as for understanding and improving generation systems themselves. We confront several questions and challenges in this work: How consistently do changing the generation outputs in predictable ways (e.g., shifting from active to passive voice) affect evaluation metric scores? Can these changes reveal systematic biases/predictable boundaries of a given metric? Are these insights truly useful above and beyond simple correlation with human judgment?

Certainly, here is my answer: Introduction Over many decades, the field of information retrieval (IR) has been committed to addressing the core problem of finding documents relevant to a user's query. Modern IR systems have largely built on the success of term-based matching, including indispensable techniques such as the now ubiquitous TF-IDF weighting (Salton et al., 1975). This approach views documents and queries as unordered sets of words, offering a simple and effective way to measure their similarity via term frequency statistics paired with the inverse document frequency, accounting for term rarity. However, this simplistic perspective keeps document semantics at a very shallow level, losing many subtleties in meaning and context, which are particularly rich in web documents today. One approach to address these limitations involves query expansion: augmenting the user's query with additional terms that are derived from documents in the semantic neighborhood of the original query terms but from which similarity to the query itself may not be as direct. Such expanded queries often improve retrieval performance (e.g., see the work of Dumais et al., 1996). Yet current methods for deciding which terms to add are somewhat ad hoc or heuristic and may often not capture the full complexity and nuance of term relationships within or even across documents. A more general goal of this research is to model the relevance space more deeply and accurately. To approach this, we consider the perspective of probabilistic generative models, while grounding this in empirical practices and requirements in IR. For a substantial time, mixture models such as latent Dirichlet allocation (Blei et al., 2003) have been applied to text modeling, especially as an unsupervised topic model for large text collections. However, such models typically operate at a corpus level, aggregating all contexts together and losing the fine-grained context of individual document collections. Here, we seek to extend and contextualize this frame for use in IR, treating queries and documents not just as bags of words, but as dynamic structured representations that capture the similarity and relations among terms in measured detail. The hierarchical Dirichlet tree, as we propose it for IR, is a way to structure the vocabulary space into a probabilistic generative model that can account for term similarity implicitly within and across document collections. The structure of a tree offers a natural and elegant way to represent similarity: leaf nodes can represent individual words, while internal nodes can store probabilistic beliefs for similarity between groups of terms.

Certainly, here is my answer: Word segmentation is one of the key preparatory steps in many natural language processing tasks. Its goal is to turn an ill-defined stream of symbols into a well-defined sequence of meaningful word-like units. The task is not trivial since languages have no ideal indispensable word boundaries or other textual delimiters; nor is there a universally accepted definition of a word. For machine translation and related tasks where one must model the relationship of source idiomatic expressions to their target language equivalents (which often vary in their constituent components fracturing or combining word boundaries), presenting words as segments with strong internal structure is an essential prerequisite. While this is a most basic NLP knowledge need, we argue that, surprisingly enough, there has been less research effort to advance such models since the latest work of (Koehn et al., 2005), even though research on semantic representation beyond words has flourished. Our goal is to propose a model that, given source/target texts and available monolingual segmentations, jointly learns to segment the source words with a view to improved bilingual translation. The key intuition is that word segmentation is similar across languages within a conceptual domain (like literary or technical writing). Even if their linguistic surface morph or derivation differs, intuitively the same concepts are segmented into roughly comparable units. Our approach, which we call "parallel guided segmentation" (PGS), leverages this intuition. Given the source text and its available monolingual segmentation, PGS learns its own source segmentation model, based on the training data. However, instead of using word-level language models like (Collins, 2002), our source segmentation model is learned as a latent in our bilingual neural translation model. During model training, when learning the parameters of our neural machine translation model, we model the joint posterior distribution over source segmentations, source-to-target alignments and the target outputs. Importantly, this setup allows our model to infer segmentations that are most suitable for translation during inference, in addition to general side tasks measured by BLEU/PARAGRAM, as demonstrated in our experiments. The proposed PGS model can leverage existing segmentations and integrate with unsupervised machine translation models, making it highly adaptable to new language pairs provided segmentations are available. Experiments conducted on English to Arabic and English to Chinese translation tasks demonstrate significant performance improvements on BLEU for our approach in comparison to baselines which either rely on manually provided word segmentation or do so without such guidance.

A foundational step for such tasks is the accurate and efficient detection of UGC, typically reviews. However, due to the diverse nature and large scale of online data, relying solely on manual labeling to identify review pages is economically infeasible and often undesirable. Instead, automatic methods for review detection have been proposed to identify review pages among web pages without human labels (Allam et al., 2013;Jindal and Liu, 2007;Zhu and Li, 2008). Historically, most automatic review detection methods have relied on a supervised learning approach similar to traditional text classification (e.g., using support vector machines, logistic regression, or any variant or derivation thereof). They typically require a labeled dataset to train a classifier and identify review pages (Jindal and Liu, 2007;Dumais et al., 2003;Pan et al., 2010). While these approaches can achieve high accuracy on datasets where labeled examples are available, they suffer from a few significant limitations. Firstly, labeling large-scale datasets manually for review detection is time-consuming and therefore can only cover a fraction of all reviews available online (Jindal and Liu, 2010). Additionally, manual labeling introduces human judgment errors and can be costly, especially for large datasets and the need to continuously update the labeled dataset as the web evolves. Furthermore, these approaches can be domain-dependent; the performance of such methods might degrade if the features in the test data differ significantly from those of the training data. For example, since product review pages may vary significantly in terminology and layout by domain (e.g., electronics, restaurants, and hotels), it can be challenging to design a single set of features that apply universally and robustly across all domains without resorting to a large, manually annotated dataset for each. These challenges have led to a need for efficient and domain-agnostic methods for review detection without relying on human labels. The utility of such an approach is obvious: researchers and practitioners can focus on developing models for more complex NLP tasks (e.g., understanding the content of reviews, or comparing reviews among different products or domains) without needing a manual review detection step as a prerequisite.

Certainly, here is my answer: Introduction Dialogue Structure Analysis (DSA) is an important task in the area of natural language processing (NLP) and computational linguistics. It involves analyzing and understanding the structure of various forms of dialogues, which range from voice-user interface dialogues (VUIs) to chatbot dialogues, human-human dialogues, clinical dialogues, and so on (Cohen and Rooth, 2010). The structure of a dialogue typically consists of turns, which can include user or system intent, context, and dialogue acts (e.g., “inform”, “query”, “negotiate”). Understanding dialogue structure can enable better knowledge extraction, decision making, and more natural conversation in applications such as question answering, human-computer interaction, and beyond. At the core of conducting DSA is the necessity to detect and accurately model relationships among semantic entities (i.e., dialogue tokens), such as utterances or partial utterances, as well as to properly structure and link those entities according to their semantic roles, intentions, and relationships within a dialogue. Traditional approaches often rely on handcrafted rules or rigid template-based systems that can suffer from limited flexibility and scalability. As dialogue corpora grow in size and diversity, both in volume and variety of domains, there is a growing need for more flexible, adaptable, and unsupervised models that can learn the structure and semantics of dialogues without extensive manual annotation. The proposed Hidden Softmax Sequence Model (HSSM) is a novel unsupervised algorithm based on the concept of the Boltzmann machine (Hinton et al., 2006) adapted for dialogue structure analysis. This work seeks to address the limitations of existing methods by introducing a novel generative neural model capable of learning latent structures of dialogues automatically. The key idea underlying HSSM is to leverage learnable latent variables to capture the underlying structures of dialogues that may not be easily inferable from textual content alone. These latent variables allow HSSM to represent the different dimensions that contribute to the structure of a dialogue, including the dependence between the meaning of adjacent utterances, the thematic context of a dialogue, and a general abstract topic that spans the entire dialogue corpus. In contrast to traditional sequence-based models such as LSTM or Transformer-based architectures that typically focus on forecasting the next token in a sequence based on previous states (e.g., for language modeling or machine translation), HSSM is specifically designed to learn dependencies, co-occurrences, and patterns that reflect dialogue structure. It operates on a sequence of utterances and internally constructs a latent representation that captures the relationships and latent structures across dialogue turns.

Training natural language parsers across multiple languages is a major challenge. A key difficulty is linguistic variability: differences in structure between languages; these are often reflected in differences in frequency distributions between word clusters (Baroni et al., 2009; Baroni and Bernardini, 2010; Erk et al., 2013; questions , 2013). Specifically, surface syntax may vary between languages (e.g., "Pronoun links" may occur more frequently in language of family 1, and "coreferential tracking" more in family 2). For example, in English, delexicalized dependency parsers (Nivre et al., 2007) have been shown to profit considerably from incorporating verbal and nominal collocation statistics (Baroni et al., 2009), even though those statistics are gathered from large unlabeled English texts. The same frequency differences are likely even more pronounced across different languages. Hence, while it is expected that such features derived from various large language-specific corpora (such as the English version of Wikipedia) could improve the accuracy of parsers, those same features cannot be directly applied (even possibly in a multi-label manner) to other languages. A related problem is cluster interference across different languages. We may have common word clusters identified from multiple languages which produce features applicable to different surface structure preferences. To leverage the linguistic structure of all languages while avoiding this problem, we propose to identify sets of word clusters that are common to multiple languages, and we show that by incorporating features extracted from these common word clusters, we are able to effectively transfer linguistic knowledge directly between languages. Instead of manually summarizing the commonality of various clusters across languages, we use unsupervised clustering of the words and their contexts across multiple large and varied language corpora. For ease of computation and real-world applicability, it is further proposed and demonstrated how to use distributional contextual embeddings (Mikolov et al., 2013; Bengio and Usrushkevich, 2009; Larsson, 2007; Baroni and Lenci, 2011) to derive rich word cluster information that incorporates both frequency and contextual co-occurrence information. While concepts such as changing the frequency distribution in transfer learning (Mou et al., 2013) have been explored, they are limited to static transfer for pre-trained dictionaries and do not directly address the structure of words as clusters. (UPDATE: This paper uses word cluster induction techniques to identify cross-language clusters and integrate them into the predictive models. These insights are based on the observations of the linguistic and structural differences observed in various languages.)

Certainly, here is the introduction for the paper on Unsupervised Neural Dependency Parsing. Dependency parsing is the task of analyzing the grammatical structure of sentences and identifying the relationships between words. It is a fundamental task in natural language processing (NLP) that provides the basis for further tasks such as named entity recognition, information extraction, and machine translation. In recent years, neural networks have become the dominant approach for dependency parsing, as they have demonstrated superior performance compared to traditional methods that use hand-crafted features and algorithms. Most state-of-the-art neural dependency parsing systems are trained using annotated data where the exact dependency structure is provided alongside the input text. This kind of knowledge is extremely valuable, but collecting such annotated data is time-consuming and expensive. As a result, there is a significant gap between the performance of dependency parsers that use annotated data and those that can operate without any explicit annotation. The task of unsupervised dependency parsing aims to bridge this gap by learning to parse without using any annotated dependency structures. Such approaches need to learn the dependency language from text where only part-of-speech (POS) tags are available. POS tags are available in larger quantities and are relatively straightforward to obtain. POS tags alone, however, provide limited detail about the syntactic or grammatical structure. They only indicate the category of each word, such as noun, verb, or adjective, but do not provide enough information to infer the exact dependency relationships between words in the sentence. Despite the challenge, unsupervised dependency parsing is a highly desirable goal because it allows dependency parsers to be applied to texts without any manual annotation. This capability would be particularly useful for languages with limited or no dependency treebanks, or for tasks where acquiring annotated data is prohibitively expensive. Additionally, unsupervised parsers could automate the process of creating and maintaining dependency treebanks, leading to a more rapid and robust NLP infrastructure. One critical challenge in unsupervised dependency parsing is finding effective ways to incorporate prior knowledge into the learning process. Prior knowledge in the context of dependency parsing typically refers to the structural preferences that words exhibit when forming dependencies. For example, base nouns acting as subjects in a sentence tend to form dependencies with verbs more frequently than other words. Previous approaches to unsupervised dependency parsing have employed various methods to encode prior knowledge. These typically involve handcrafted features or pre-defined prior distributions over grammar rules.

Training neural machine translation (NMT) models with a large vocabulary is computationally expensive due to the cost of computing softmax probabilities. In this paper, we propose a novel method to reduce the computation cost using binary codes rather than probability distributions. The main idea is to predict a binary code for each word in the target language vocabulary instead of a distribution over the vocabulary. In the best case, this reduces the computation time/memory requirements of the output layer to be logarithmic in the vocabulary size. This makes the inference and training of NMT models much more efficient. Table 1 (left) outlines the major challenges of NMT and how our proposed approach address these challenges. We further introduce two error-correcting techniques, using Reed-Solomon codes and combining softmax and binary codes, to improve the robustness of our system. Experimental results on two English to Japanese translation tasks show that our methods can achieve performance comparable to the state-of-the-art softmax-based models while making significant improvements in computation speed and memory usage. 2. MODEL OVERVIEW A standard encoder-decoder NMT model computes the probability distribution of the translation output over the entire vocabulary using a softmax layer at the last layer of the model. As the vocabulary size increases, the computation cost and memory usage also increase, making it more difficult to train and use NMT on large vocabularies (e.g., millions of different words). One solution to reduce the computation cost is to replace the softmax layer with a binary code layer. In the binary coding approach, we predict a distinct binary code for each word in the vocabulary. Given the output of the neural network (e.g., from the previous layer), we binarize it using an appropriate binarization scheme (e.g., bitwise rounding) and map the binarized result to a codeword. Table 2 illustrates the approach: in the softmax-based model (left), the output of the last layer is a vector of size V, where each element represents the logits for a word in the vocabulary. On the other side of the table, in the binary code approach (right), the last layer produces a vector of binary values (0's and 1's) of size log2(V) which are then mapped to distinct and unique codewords. To reconstruct a word from the binary code, we can use a simple codebook lookup or a decoder that maps a series of binary digits back to the original words.

This problem has various applications, including information retrieval (IR) and conversational systems. These pairs are considered to be well-formed answers to the questions and are used as training data, which is the foundation of DS-QA. Despite its usefulness, DS-QA still faces several challenges. The first is the noisiness of distantly supervised data. Past research has shown that such data often contain many incorrect or irrelevant answers. In addition, different types of questions might have different answer extraction mechanisms, further complicating the extent to which distantly supervised data can be equated to the target task's answers. The contextual information from other paragraphs, especially for convoluted questions requiring answer aggregation or inference, could prove crucial. In this paper, we propose a denoising, context-aware framework for DS-QA that directly addresses these issues. Specifically, we couple paragraph selection with answer extraction. Decisions ranging from what movies to watch, where to travel, to even determining the best book to read are often influenced by search results. However, web search quality drastically varies across languages, even though the intent of the user questions remains the same. This disparity in quality leads to suboptimal search experiences for users querying in less popular languages or when querying in the dominant (e.g., English) language for globally relevant results. Problems and Motivation For example, an English user searching for “Chinese medieval history” might get primarily English language documents, omitting vast troves of highly relevant content written in Chinese. These documents, often produced by native Chinese speakers, contain in-depth knowledge that might not be as available in English. Similarly, a Chinese user searching in Chinese language for “American Thanksgiving traditions” would likely get results from Chinese websites written for Chinese audience. However, certain information, such as the latest historical studies or cultural nuances, might only be available in English literature. Despite advances in cross-language information retrieval (CLIR), web search often falls short when it comes to providing consistent, quality search results across languages. CLIR techniques often focus on translating queries or documents between languages, which can be ineffective for complex search queries or less common languages with shallow resources. Where CLIR succeeds, the resulting retrievements can still suffer in relevance compared to a search performed natively in the target language [Christian et al. 2002]. A Potential Solution: Bilingual Information A potential solution to bridge this gap is to leverage bilingual search queries and bilingual page content. Bilingual search queries are queries that represent the same search interest in different languages, such as “French medieval history” (English) and “法语中世纪历史” (Chinese). Bilingual content refers to textual data (web pages, documents) available in multiple languages. The general idea is to harness the information in these bilingual pairs to improve search results. Firstly, by understanding the translation patterns between bilingual documents, we can better handle queries in both languages, possibly through improved term translation, or by ranking bilingual content together to capture concepts that might not be well represented in monolingual results. Secondly, bilingual query pairs allow us to learn from variations in user queries across languages for the same topic. For instance, when users in different languages search for broadly the same thing (e.g., global news, technology products), subtle differences in phrasing or terminology might be predictive of what constitutes more relevant content in one language versus another.

Automated short-answer grading is key to helping close the automation loop for large-scale, online testing in education. It can provide instantaneous feedback and automate the process of assessing large batches of open-ended questions. While significant advances have been made in this area (e.g. Lai and Potts, 2015;Ashley, 2007), there remains a gap in our understanding of how different feature types and linguistic levels of processing contribute to automated short-answer grading. Specifically, current state-of-the-art techniques often implicitly use various feature types, but there has been little rigorous investigation of which feature types are most useful and when. This is due in part to the challenges of comparative evaluation, as different datasets and task contexts can lead to varying conclusions. Moreover, recent advances have introduced powerful natural language processing techniques that leverage neural networks and deep learning (e.g. Devlin et al., 2018; Radford et al., 2018) which may have redefined the exploration of which feature types are most useful. Furthermore, different tasks and datasets also require different levels of linguistic scrutiny. In educational assessment, for example, content knowledge and conceptual understanding are often probed beyond mere lexical and syntactic correctness, relying on semantic or even inferential understanding. For instance, a question asking a student to identify symbols of a culture might require not just lexical recall of the expected answer, but an understanding of cultural context or the ability to generate semantically related answers. In English language assessment, a student might be asked to identify the mood in a given passage, or to paraphrase a text, tasks that require higher levels of semantic understanding. Consequently, this study aims to provide a comprehensive and comparative evaluation of different feature types across various levels of linguistic representation, and across contexts that elicit different kinds of short answers. First, we will investigate feature types across three levels of linguistic processing: lexical, syntactic, and semantic. The lexical level includes textual features such as word frequency, term frequency-inverse document frequency (TF-IDF), or the presence of specific words or patterns. The syntactic level includes structural features like part-of-speech tag counts, dependency parse metrics, or sentence length. Latent Variable PCFGs (Asr and Collins, 2005; Blunsom et al., 2005) can capture such latent structure implicitly and outperform standard PCFGs on parsing tasks. The primary benefit of latent variables is that they allow a grammar to capture latent structure while remaining succinct, reducing the number of grammar rules and hence the size of the vocabulary. These models, however, introduce a new layer of complexity in two areas. First, latent-variable distributions impose an additional component to the decoding problem, in the form of a latent-variable recognition task. Second, the learning problem is no longer purely parametric. The expected probability of a parse tree, known as the marginal likelihood, is not tractable, and hence we rely on approximations. In the past, latent-variable PCFGs have been trained using greedy EM-like algorithms, or by running decoding with a greedy search or a beam search. While these methods perform reasonably well in practice on standard treebanks, they lack theoretical groundings and hence justification for expected results. As a language learner progresses, the recognition of "hello" as a greeting might evolve from purely recognizing it as a certain collection of sounds/letters into its being used appropriately in different conversation settings, its creative variations, idiomatic expressions, synonyms, and antonyms. This deepening understanding of a word suggests that the "knowledge" of a word or a concept has different stages or "maturities".
