While the count-based metrics like word frequency and other corpus-based methods (Antonia et al., 2009;Sethuraman & Liang, 2007) are significantly correlated with empirical word difficulty as measured through reading comprehension or vocabulary tests, they have limitations (1) in that they do not account for the variability in language learning trajectories across different ages/stages and (2) fail to capture the potential "semantic depth" of word knowledge. The concept of word maturity, on the other hand, aims to capture the degree of knowledge about a word from naive, early beginner-level recognition to sophisticated, deep understanding of the word as a component in a vast array of cognitive and linguistic contexts. Social media platforms, such as Reddit, provide a wealth of public discussions across various topics. Dogmatism in this context can be defined as the reluctance to consider alternative viewpoints and the tendency to rely on a set of rigidly held beliefs. Identifying and mitigating dogmatism in social media conversations can lead to healthier and more productive discussions, facilitating a better understanding of complex issues and reducing polarization. We hypothesize that dogmatic comments exhibit certain distinctive features, which can be quantified and tracked over time. Dogmatic individuals are overconfident in their beliefs, resistant to arguments that contradict these beliefs, and display a reluctance to engage in cognitive or mental processes that might challenge their perspective (Ray, 1973). Existing literature has explored these characteristics using different metrics and self-report questionnaires. However, extending these findings to the context of online discourse presents new challenges in operationalizing the concept and its evaluation within a textual, dynamic, and often anonymous environment. ### Methodology We utilize a corpus of Reddit posts annotated for dogmatism through a paid, crowdsourced annotation process. Our labeling process asks annotators to score each post on several dimensions reflecting key aspects of dogmatism, such as overconfidence, perceived rigidity, and lack of open-mindedness. This data allows us to train models that can identify dogmatic posts based on both linguistic signals and behavioral patterns. #### Linguistic Signals: - Use of absolute language or the lack of nuanced thought - Reference to, or lack of, evidence or consideration of alternative viewpoints - High reliance on abstract terminology or emotionally charged language - Absence of confronting dissonant information or engaging with counterarguments #### Behavioral Patterns: - Post frequency on divisive or sensitive topics - User engagement style, such as repetitive posting or aggressive interaction habits - Self-assessment of the user’s behavior when expressing belief changes or reconsidering viewpoints ### Model Development Our model is based on a combination of textual and behavioral features, leveraging techniques from natural language processing and behavioral data modeling.

Training deep neural networks can be computationally expensive, and this prohibits achieving performance improvements using large-scale deep neural networks unless a significant number of training examples is available (Hung and Vu, 2005). In practice, many datasets used in NLP are small-to-medium sized and indispensable for improving the performance of deep models trained on a smaller labeled dataset. A questions remains as to how to best utilize the available unlabeled data to improve model performance. One way to approach this problem is through semi-supervised learning, of which the goal is to build a model that leverages both labeled and unlabeled data during training. Traditionally, semi-supervised text classification has focused on exploiting word co-occurrence patterns within unlabeled text examples to improve performance (Chapelle et al., 2006;Hoffmann, 2001;Turian et al., 2008). Text sequences or paragraphs can be modeled by using shallow, linear classifiers to capture document-level features and achieve certain success on supervised data, but its performance on large-scale, deep NLP tasks, such as text classification, remains limited due to the inability to model complex sentence structures and hierarchical features. Deep models, such as sequential neural networks, capable of modeling complex sentence structures and capturing long-range dependencies can potentially improve performance on NLP tasks. Recent work shows that deep models can achieve state-of-the-art performance on a variety of NLP tasks including POS tagging (Srivastava et al., 2015), language modeling (Pennington et al., 2014;Dai and Le, 2015), sentence simplification, and summarization (Chen et al., 2015;Nallapati et al., 2016). However, due to their large number of parameters, they require a large labeled dataset for training (He et al., 2016). Therefore, to benefit from large unlabeled datasets and yet maintain performance gain on a smaller labeled dataset, the semi-supervised approach is a natural choice, provided that the right strategy for leveraging unlabeled data is used. Nonetheless, explicitly leveraging rich unstructured information present in large amounts of unlabeled data remains challenging. While discriminative deep models can generally be trained more efficiently on large amounts of data, semi-supervised learning approaches – typically borrowed from unsupervised learning – often experience difficulty in maintaining and improving the discriminative capacity of the model throughout the training process. A key challenge with current semi-supervised approaches is the need for strong theoretical justification of the use of unlabeled data in deep neural networks. This challenge stems partly from the fact that deep networks are highly expressive and, without explicit regularization or control over the learning process, may learn features that are more useful for fitting the data than capturing generalizable patterns.

Named Entity Recognition (NER) involves tagging specific types of entities present in unstructured texts. Traditionally, NER models are trained exclusively on source domain data, and such models normally suffer a significant performance drop when applied to target domains with various linguistic characteristics. In this work, we propose a Domain Adaptation (DA) method, named as Latent Semantic Association (LaSA), to significantly alleviate the domain shift problem in NER without any access to labeled target domain data. The basic intuition behind LaSA is to capture latent semantic association among words from an unlabeled corpus, and use it for bridging data distribution gap between source and target domains. The latent semantic association knowledge is first learned from an unlabeled corpus through a lazy association learning model. Specifically, for every word, we first extract its features based on a certain context. Then we group the derived feature vectors into multiple semantic concepts via a subspace clustering algorithm, which ignores concept labels but focuses on identifying the latent semantic structure. For domain adaptation, we project the source and target word spaces to the concept space via learned association knowledge, such that equivalent terms in different domains could be mapped to the same concept, while various domain-specific terms are discerned. As for the sequential structure of sentences, we propose a matrix-based scoring function that effectively combines the uniform context vector representation and the relevance between semantic units obtained from latent semantic association learning. Then, we specifically adapt a BiLSTM-CRF model for NER to the new space defined by the association concept vectors. Our algorithm not only can effectively transfer the labeled information from source domain to target domain without compromising the inference capability of NER model, but significantly reduces domain shift by disentangling different semantic meanings of the same terms. We evaluate the proposed LaSA-based DA method on English and Chinese NER datasets across multiple domains. Experimental results show that our method outperforms the state-of-the-art DA methods which generally require labeled target data, including cross-entropy, label smoothing and zero-shot learning methods. Furthermore, LaSA method shares no variables with those DA methods that require labeled target data, thus achieving compatibility for practical scenarios where labeled data is insufficient or expensive. The following paper is organized as follows. We first introduce related works in Section 2. In Section 3, we present details of our proposal including latent semantic association learning and domain adaptation with concept space.

Training neural machine translation (NMT) models for multiple language pairs simultaneously has recently been an area of research interest (Dzmitryx Danylushkin, 2016;Moses et al., 2017). These multilingual NMT models aim to achieve the best of both worlds: benefiting from shared knowledge across multiple languages while accounting for language-specific differences (Liu and Monz, 2017). A key component of NMT that makes this shared and specialized language learning possible is the attention mechanism (Bahdanau et al., 2015), which keeps track of how information flows between different parts of the input sentence and output sentence word-by-word. This attention mechanism has been shown to significantly improve translation quality (Luong et al., 2015), but so far, most work applies a single attention mechanism for all language pairs, even in a multilingual setup. This "one-size-fits-all" attention might have limitations. Languages with certain syntactic structures or semantic properties might require different configurations of attention, for instance, languages where order of words in a sentence is more important might require an attention mechanism that deals with hierarchical or top-down attention, or languages with rich morphology might benefit from attention mechanisms that cluster related word-forms together. To address this, and to see if task or language specificity can further improve multilingual NMT, we introduce task-specific attention, while retaining the parameter sharing across all language pairs. Stated more formally, our model allows to independently fine-tune an attention model for each language pair or translation task, without compromising the multi-language generalization (as opposed to having one unique learned attention model per language pair). The intuition behind this approach is that even though certain parameters of the attention mechanism might be shared across all languages (allowing for generalization across languages), some might learn better with fine-tuning tailored to the specific structure of input sentences or the nuances of the vocabulary in particular languages. This approach can be seen as a middle ground between fully shared and fully independent models, where together with shared parameters, we allow for limited, task-specific specialization. The architecture is detailed in Section 2.1, and we argue in Section 2.2 why this framework should work, and what it inherits from previous methods. In Section 3, we present experiments on 4 languages from the Europarl corpus, showing consistent gains for all language pairs when using task-specific attention, across both directions of translation, including zero-shot (unseen at training time) translation directions.

Named Entity Recognition (NER) involves detecting and classifying named entities mentioned in unstructured text into predefined categories. Traditionally, NER systems are trained and evaluated on specific domains such as news articles, academic papers, or webpages, and their performance degrades when applied to different domains. For instance, the NER system trained on news articles is likely to perform poorly on clinical texts or web queries. This degradation is often due to domain-specific linguistic phenomena, terminology, idioms, and stylistic variations which are not covered by the training data of the NER system. Thus, adapting NER systems to different domains remains a challenging task in natural language processing. Several approaches have been proposed to tackle cross-domain NER. Some methods rely on feature engineering to identify domain-dependent features and adjust the NER model based on these features. Sentiment analysis (Hovy and Gerber, 2009) and domain-specific word embeddings (Wang et al., 2015) have been used to achieve this. Another approach leverages the large amount of text data available across different domains and employs ensemble methods to combine predictions from multiple NER models trained on similar text data. However, these methods often require careful selection of features or training of multiple models, or depend on the availability of labeled data from the target domain. The problem becomes particularly problematic when dealing with out-of-domain text data where the expected named entities may be rare or absent in the training data. For instance, adapting an NER system trained on news articles to classify entities in web queries can be challenging due to differences in language style, abbreviations, colloquialisms, and pseudonyms often used in web queries, all of which are not adequately represented in news articles. Named Entity Recognition (NER) involves detecting and classifying named entities mentioned in unstructured text into predefined categories such as persons, organizations, and locations. State-of-the-art NER systems typically rely on deep neural networks (DNNs) and various forms of feature engineering, including the use of large annotated corpora and language-specific resources, such as gazetteers and syntax-based features. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel NER model that can operate with limited or no task-specific features in source or target languages, enabling quick adaptation to new languages or domains with minimal additional training data. The proposed model's core innovation lies in its use of phonologically aware neural features. While traditional NER methods heavily rely on orthographic tokens (e.g., individual characters or whole words), our model leverages phonological character representations and word embeddings to capture more nuanced linguistic patterns amenable to transfer between languages. Our phonologically aware neural model, which we term the "Phonologically Aware Neural Model for Named Entity Recognition" or PAN for short, is designed to perform robustly even in low resource transfer settings where only a small amount of annotated target language data might be available. The PAN model incorporates an attention mechanism to dynamically interact between the phonological features of the input text and the classification task of NER. By using phonologically informed representations, we aim to identify patterns and structures at a deeper level of language than mere surface orthography, facilitating cross-lingual transfer despite lacking language-specific pre-training or feature engineering. The use of phonological representations is motivated by several key insights. First, many languages share common phonological structures and patterns, which can be leveraged for transfer learning. Second, phonological features can capture word patterns more robustly than orthographic features, especially in languages with complex spelling or script systems (e.g., Arabic or Chinese). Third, unlike whole-word embeddings or orthographic representations, phonological representations are relatively language-neutral and can be applied across a wide range of languages with minimal adaptation. A key component of PAN is its attentional mechanism, which evaluates the relevance of phonological features across different segments of input text to the NER task. This mechanism allows the model to selectively focus on those parts of the input that most influence the correct identification of named entities.

A better strategy may be to follow a curriculum that makes the representation more useful for tasks of increasing difficulty (Rosenbaum et al., 2006). For example, character-based segmentation can be a useful preprocessing for Chinese NLP tasks (Sun et al., 2010). However, learning a curriculum requires a form of problem-internal supervision that informs the learner of what training instances are more and less difficult. While labeling each word as to its difficulty in the sample is impossible, we can use the corpus to self-supervise this learning process. One strategy is to rank words or contexts based on some engineered feature vector (Ranganath et al., 2015) describing their complexity and build a curriculum according to this rank (Collobert et al., 2011;Weinberger, 2000;Alex et al., 2010;Chelba et al., 2013). A linear ordering of all words while the system learns can be useful for the entire downstream set at the end, however it may also overlook the training dynamics at individual point in time and may keep certain very difficult instances in the current training (but not yet in generalization set) stage. Evolutionary methods can in principle be used to search for an optimal curriculum, by trying different learning orders and measuring performance improvements and they are especially useful when the curriculum is task-specific (Risi, 2010;Poli, 2008;Langdon et al., 2009). While such methods appear promising in general artificial intelligence, they may be hard to apply to real-world tasks of the variety we are interested in because of their computational requirements. Curricula explicitly built for tasks have shown performance improvements in word embeddings (Xue et al., 2017) and byte-pair encoding (Sennrich et al., 2017). For example, some investigations suggest that in complex tasks like multi-choice reading comprehension, it can be useful to follow a ranking such as: nouns $\rightarrow$ named entities $\rightarrow$ proper nouns $\rightarrow$ pronouns (Rajpurkar et al., 2016;Rajpurkar et al., 2018). There is no formally proven way to obtain a universally optimal curriculum for all architectures and tasks. However, we still wish to optimize the curriculum internally during training to improve performance on target tasks without resorting to finding a globally optimal order offline that may not generalize well to any specific model or task.

Training natural language processing (NLP) models optimize a loss function that is often first order. However, these models are usually evaluated using more complex metrics that capture second and third order aspects of the data, such as ROUGE and BLEU for sequence-to-sequence tasks like machine translation. A particular challenge comes from the need to maximize accuracy for instance on questions or answers while being evaluated over the whole dialogue or text. This misalignment between the optimization and evaluation can often lead to a suboptimal representation and therefore to worse generalization or performance on downstream tasks. Two common methods to address this gap are policy gradients and curriculum learning (Elbayad and Jurafsky, 2018;Kumar, 2016;Bapst and Kolter, 2018). The former directly optimizes a loss that is differentiable but derived from an evaluation metric. This approach, however, can be computationally expensive and has a high variance making the policy gradient training unstable. Hence, while it is expected to optimize the sequence-level problem better, it often performs worse than the MLE baseline. Curriculum learning, on the other hand, builds up progressively harder training problems but it is often black box and lacks interpretability. One intermediate approach towards addressing the problem is to intuitively define a sequentially differentiable adversarial objective on the output symbols. Recent work in this line uses different training objectives for each output symbol but this may overfit, while another approach attempts to map label sequences to sets of output sequences and uses a mixture of objectives, one for the individual output correctness and another to measure their sequential structure overfit. Another class of current approaches (Li et al., 2019;Ahram and Sprague, 2019) reformulate the optimization problem and directly focus on sequence structure and "long-term goals" but still likely doesn't learn a robust, global loss that captures the sequence structure well. In this paper, we propose an alternative approach to policy gradients and curriculum learning by approximating the longest common subsequence (LCS) between reference and generated sequences. We approximate the LCS function with a differentiable surrogate. We call our approach CALCS, or Continuously Approximating Longest Common Subsequence for Sequence Level Optimization and describe a systematic extension of LCS to changing sequence generation where we add a moving window analogy to approximate LCS on large sequences. We use this approximated LCS for sequence level optimization during training. Our proposed CALCS objective works by estimating structure over a window of recent input/output pairs while also capturing global sequence similarity.

Introduction Natural language inference (NLI) is a core problem in natural language processing (NLP): given two sentences, one of which is the hypothesis and the other the premise, the goal is to determine the logical relationship between them, such as entailment, contradiction, or neutral (Ehret and Ngomo, 2016; Bowman et al., 2015). Recent advances in deep learning have led to significant improvements in solving NLI with neural networks, with an accuracy that approaches human performance. A key component of these models is the ability to capture long-range dependencies between the hypothesis and the premise, which can be viewed as a task of interaction between features of the sentences. This is often accomplished by mechanisms derived from or inspired by the concept of attention, in which a context-dependent “linear combination” of sentence features is taken to compute an alignment score or even a subset of the features most relevant to predict the relationship (Cheng et al., 2020;Radford et al., 2019;Hu et al., 2017). However, relying on attention or variants thereof has several limitations For one, attention-based models can be unstable or inefficient when dealing with long sequences (Dai et al., 2016) and sometimes lack the explicit modeling of interaction between sentence features in a more structured and flexible way than simple linear combinations, which are the core of attention mechanisms. Another limitation is that using attention necessitates a specific inference structure based on previous work: typically an additive combination of features is used to predict the relationship, but this is not based on a strong general principle, and the model must learn the interaction "from scratch" even when the underlying task might suggest a more structured approach. Last but not the least, given how recent attention mechanisms have been, including but not limited to, dynamic or structured attention (Liu et al., 2019; Kafle and Kanich, 2018), there is little understanding of their general applicability or robustness advantages in various tasks or datasets. A different direction to capture sentence interaction could be via filters or convolutions, a concept directly borrowed from computer vision where large amounts of spatial data (such as images) are processed using filters to extract local features. Convolution in natural language processing has been fruitful in modeling local dependencies (Kim, 2014), semantic tasks (Peters et al., 2019; Johnson and Zhang, 2015), and has shown potential in few-shot learning for classification (Gulcehre et al., 2018) and other tasks.

Corpus Domain: For domains where the structure of sentences follows certain predictable patterns (e.g., reviews about restaurants), syntactic patterns could work better. Training natural language parsers typically involves reranking candidate parse trees. A strict reranking criterion's cost function is engineered specifically to address a particular task and language pair. Domain knowledge and computational heuristics may help guide choice of the cost function. Most parsers are developed for tasks with ideal labels (e.g. parse trees annotated by humans). For example, in phrase questions , the task is to predict the answer given a question sentence and a context (e.g., "What did John buy?", given the sentences "John bought milk at the store." and "He purchased vegetables too."). Gold-standard annotated parse trees provide exact labels to guide training and inference. However, in many natural language applications, we are interested in using language for complex tasks such as question answering, summarization, and machine translation, where we don't haveaccess to gold-standard labeled data (or have limited labeled data). For example, we can't derive a gold-standard parse tree for the "navigation answer" from the parser's output because we have no reference parse tree for such a complex task. This problem is especially true in grounded language acquisition, which seeks to learn mappings between words and meanings grounded in perception. For instance, in the task of instruction following, the goal is to learn what or where to go given a navigation instruction (e.g., "Go to the kitchen"). The task requires understanding not just the syntactic structure of the sentence, but also its semantic interpretation in the context of the visual scene. If the learning system goes to the wrong place, it is considered incorrect, but we cannot directly obtain an annotated parse tree indicating exactly why (e.g., whether the system misunderstood "kitchen" as "bathroom" or whether it interpreted the instruction as "go to the living room first, then the kitchen"). We might achieve corrections with feedback (e.g., "Wrong answer: doesn't go to the kitchen" or "Feedback is inconsistent with the input"). Feedback does not directly provide a gold-standard parse tree, but if one is clever, feedback could possibly be less noisy or more measured, helping in reranking a probabilistic parse, for instance, by penalizing certain components of the parse. Nonetheless, explicitly defining a reranking cost function that incorporates feedback implicitly or explicitly and is also systematic (e.g., based on a probabilistic model that aligns with the task semantics) requires a structured approach to leverage the sparse and indirect guidance provided by feedback.

The dataset contains a wide range of navigation instructions and several different environments, including simple corridors and maze-like configurations. The encoding network first constructs two contextual vectors based on the user instruction and the map. Next, we couple this contextual vector with a feature vector from a convolutional neural network (CNN) that represents the entire environment map. The decoding network then generates the navigation plan step-by-step. At every step of decoding, the attention mechanism focuses on parts of the map and parts of the instruction that are relevant for generating the next step in the plan.

ZSAR is important due to its ability to generalize and be practically useful, as in many scenarios, video labels are difficult or expensive to obtain (e.g., a company may want to automatically classify some kind of activity that isn't categorized yet). Another difficulty is the linguistic challenge: action verbs often have multiple meanings and carry certain associations, which should be used to infer properties of actions, yet sometimes these meanings are not explicitly captured in the definitions provided by dictionaries and require an abstract interpretation. For instance, "throwing" suggests a certain type of physical motion and presumably deals with throwing something. While the action itself can be universally recognized on a basic level (i.e., it includes the motion of an object being propelled through the air), specific details such as the type of object, the precision of the motion, or its social implication (e.g., "throw a ball at a friend" or "throw a grenade at an enemy") depend on specific attributes that could vary significantly, especially if we consider throwing different objects in different contexts as new categories. Verb attributes, derived from the lexical contexts and meanings of action verbs, can serve as a bridge between the visual and linguistic representations, providing the necessary abstraction and the ability to reason about unseen actions. If attributes such as "light movement", "social act", or "dynamic decision-making" can be reliably inferred for known verbs and used to predict these attributes for unseen verbs, it would be possible to generate confident predictions about the nature of activities described by verbs without explicit training data. This paper presents a novel approach to ZSAR that leverages verb attribute induction from dictionaries and large-scale word embeddings. The model learns to map action verbs to a set of attributes that capture their visual, social, or behavioral properties.

For search query processing, it is important to disambiguate these cases to retrieve relevant documents. This necessitates accurate annotations. These alternative methods include, but are not limited to, measures that directly evaluate how well human evaluators would perceive and rate the proposed output (e.g., the human-computer communication (HCC) measure), or creative automatic metrics (e.g., the Persuasion Rate (Persuasion Rate (pass)), the Human-Score for Evaluation of Summaries (HES)) or cluster-based techniques For Human Evaluation of Text (CHET and CHET++), or RiTa for poetry generation). Even the n-gram based techniques have been assumed, while the 'diversity' of the n-gram units over the evaluation set (as, e.g., computed by the ROUGE measure or by using distinct n-gram units), contributes to the 'perceived quality' of the summarization (Ahrndt and Ng, 2006;Ahrndt and Ng, 2007). Other n-gram based approaches, such as BLEU 2 or BLEU 3, which consider contextual information and the use of cross-source n-gram based evaluation (as suggested by the METEOR measure or the measured evaluation methods in Machine Translation research), also fall into the above group. For the more complex NLP tasks, even cognitive or psycholinguistic factors have been incorporated in evaluation measures . While many of these methods have been introduced with a task in mind, and in some cases (summarization, translation, speech recognition, interactive systems evaluation, etc.) some are also used in evaluations for other tasks, they broadly lack adoption. The reasons for this are probably varied. Some of the proposed measures have not yet been sufficiently thoroughly tested or validated to have gained the theoretical background that could have led to more acceptance in practice.

Training neural models directly from question-answer pairs has led to state of the art performance on question answering (QA) datasets; these models have become core components of modern knowledge base question answering systems. To address this issue, this paper proposes "Neural Compositional Denotational Semantics," an end-to-end differentiable model that learns to represent the meaning of spans of text as both denotations in a given knowledge graph and ungrounded latent vectors, and uses this to perform compositional reasoning. The model is inspired by formal semantics such as dynamic semantics and Montague's intensional logic (Montague, 1974) and integrates insights from computational semantics research. It addresses a number of recent challenges in the area: the need for better generalization to complex questions and the requirement of handling underspecified or incomplete linguistic input. This model uses an augmented version of the graph neural network (GNN) (Scarselli et al., 2009) to learn a denotational semantics representation for any span or subgraph in the KG. For each span this representation consists of both a grounded denotation (a graph representation that is a function of the shallow text-to-KG alignment assumed in the model) and an ungrounded latent vector that allows for encoding its meaning within a vector space (Figure 1). A key insight in this design is using distinct vectors for distinct span types (e.g., for functional predicates like "near", or for entities like "New York"). Assuming a question is composed of a number of spans (e.g., "Which "city" "goes with" doesn't "apply" "almost no" "green park"?"), the model recursively composes the semantics of these spans using learned composition operators (Figure 2). Each operator takes two or three span semantics representations, modifies their vectors, and combines the denotations of the spans. For example, a "not" operator would negate the value of a vector representing some attribute of one span, or disjunction would combine span vectors via a weighted average. To capture potential ambiguity and diverse syntactic structure of questions, we build a parse chart (Section 2 for details) in which for every multi-token span in the question we consider several competing interpretations (e.g., different semantic roles for "city" as subject or object of a relation).

Historical documents, especially those from past centuries, are frequently filled with strictures such as archaic spellings, obsolete shorthand, and varied orthographic conventions. Generally speaking, two goals are often pursued when dealing with such documents: (1) diplomatic transcription, which seeks to preserve the original orthography of the document as closely as possible, and (2) normalized transcription, which pursues the creation of a standardized orthography, useful for most downstream NLP tasks and human readability. At first glance, these two objectives might appear to be somewhat at odds with each other - normalization often implies a degree of reinterpretation of the original text, whereas diplomatic transcription strives to maintain the original form. However, a comprehensive solution could ideally provide both simultaneously: a method that learns to recognize the original orthography and executes a probabilistic mapping between it and a modern, normalized form. This paper proposes a novel, unsupervised model that addresses this challenge. The core idea is to develop a deep learning-based framework capable of learning orthographic variation directly from the data without the need for explicit labels or supervision for either the original or the modern orthography symbols. Our model is based on a multitask architecture where the network learns two tasks in tandem: 1. Recognizing the written symbols in the historical text with respect to its original, varied orthography. 2. Mapping these symbols (or groups thereof) to their equiva-lents in modern English orthography. To achieve this, we employ deep neural networks in conjunction with a variant of generative adversarial networks (GANs) optimized for sequence transduction and mapping over variable length inputs. The model doesn't learn a simple, 1-to-1 mapping but instead captures distributional regularities and patterns of orthographic variation over the document. The architecture includes: - A sub-network that focuses on the recognition task, modeling the probabilistic distribution of symbols, their sequences, and their variations within the context of the historical document. - A parallel sub-network or layer tasked with learning the distribution of mappings from historical to modern orthographies. - A loss function that distinguishes between plausibility of the hypothesized original orthography and the quality of the mapped modern form. The unsupervised training objective encourages the model to learn a self-consistent set of mappings and symbol distributions.

Training Data Quality is key to the success of Machine Learning (ML) systems (Guizzo et al., 2011). However, designing and developing high quality training data is often expensive and time-consuming (Grauman, 2005). However, the labeling accuracy of non-expert annotators can vary significantly, degrading the quality and reliability of the resulting data even if an individual labeler's performance is not particularly bad. An accuracy error rate of 10% for a hypothetical lazy or malicious annotator does not initially seem like a big problem, but even this small fraction of bad labels can have a surprisingly large impact on labeling accuracy for the entire corpus. As shown below, in a large corpus with 10, 000 labeled instances and 20% of those labels being from a single bad annotator with 10% error, we would expect to have 2, 000 bad labels. If we assume this error introduces a contradictory or simply inconsistent label compared to the rest or even adds some noise, the total overall labeling accuracy would drop from 0.9 (assuming no errors otherwise) to as low as 0.76. Modifying the system to handle such issues can be particularly challenging if the data acquisition process uses a mixture of different, potentially untrusted, data sources. Learning to trust annotators, or more precisely, learning which annotators to trust, is an important problem in acquiring and maintaining high quality labeled data sets. The key is not only to determine the accuracy of annotations, but also to do so efficiently and effectively. Here we present a system, MACE (Multi-Annotator Competence Estimation), which learns which annotators are reliable and which are not using an item-response model (IRT) (Lord and Novick, 1968). Our primary objective of the MACE system is to a) identify which annotators are trustworthy, and b) accurately predict the correct underlying labels . While MACE is generally applicable to any annotation setting, we'll apply and evaluate it within the context of code tagging, a core problem in programming language research that requires identifying the role or function of each code token (Binkley, 1995). (UPDATE: This paper uses real AMT data to report the effectiveness of MACE and establish baselines against state-of-the-art methods.) An extensive amount of research has been conducted into trust and competence estimation, particularly within the context of crowdsourced classification tasks (Karger et al., 2008; Bhattacharyya et al., 2010; Ipeirotis et al., 2010).

A key finding from these works is that modeling relation paths (i.e., sequences of one or more relations) contributes to the performance of these models, suggesting that the way entities are connected in a KB contributes meaning and increases prediction accuracy. For example, an embedding model can capture the representation of "Steve Jobs" by looking at his direct relations, but also by considering lazy paths – paths assembled through repeated applications of the "has company" relation – such as "Steve Jobs" -> "Apple" -> ... -> "Google". This ability to look at multiple paths from one entity to another can capture various semantic relationships, and has led to improved accuracy in KB completion tasks (e.g., predicting known and unknown relations between entities). However, handling relation paths in practical ways has been a challenge. For similar relations in various applications (e.g., "has company" between multiple companies), enumerating all or even a significant fraction of possible paths between two given entities can be computationally prohibitive. Most existing approaches attempt to address this by sampling a subset of paths (Bordes et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2014a; Sun et al., 2016). This approximation can lead to missing certain valuable information (e.g., specific, perhaps rare, paths that contain critical insight for predicting certain relations), and can be particularly limiting for more complex, longer relation paths. Moreover, if we aim to model text jointly with KBs (situations where text contains candidates for KBs and is the primary evidence for KB completion), incorporating path information can be even more convoluted. We can't assume that texts directly reference entities or relations that the KB has; in fact, a single piece of text often touches upon many concepts and relations that may not be explicitly mentioned in the KB but are evident through inference over relations in the KB. For instance, a sentence might mention a company merger but not the date. With relation paths, we can infer such a date by considering paths such as "merger between companies" -> "a complex event instantiated between them and lasting over time". However, directly eliciting such interpretation from text requires sophisticated zero-shot or few-shot relational reasoning, an area still under active research (Riedel et al., 2013; Bordes et al., 2011; Misra et al., 2015).

Recognizing Implicit Discourse Relations via Repeated Reading: Neural Networks with Multi-Level Attention Abstract Differentiating between implicit and explicit discourse relations has been a longstanding challenge in natural language processing. While explicit discourse relations are well-expressed using linguistic features such as discourse connectives, implicit relations are only inferred through the interplay of content clauses and do not have explicit markers. To tackle this challenge, we propose a novel model, Neural Networks with Multi-Level Attention (NNMA), which mimics the process of repeated reading where the argumentative text is iteratively processed and examined for important linguistic features that hint at the underlying discourse relation. The model employs a multi-level attention mechanism along with external memory to capture and assemble linguistic feature representations incrementally at each stage of repeated reading. The attention mechanism guides the model to focus on the most relevant parts of the text as it reads the arguments multiple times. At each iteration, the model can adjust its attention to different parts of the text based on what it has learned so far, much like how a human being might go back and read a challenging text multiple times to better understand the underlying meaning. Our evaluation on the PDTB (Penn Discourse TreeBank) dataset for implicit discourse relations demonstrates that the NNMA model achieves state-of-the-art results. We also provide a visualization of the attention weights, showing how the model progressively focuses on specific parts of the text during repeated readings, highlighting the importance of this approach. The key contributions of this work are twofold: (i) We introduce the concept of repeated reading using a neural network architecture to recognize implicit discourse relations, which has not been explored before in this context, and (ii) We leverage multi-level attention and external memory to gradually refine the model's understanding of the discourse structure at multiple levels. 1 Introduction Discourse analysis is crucial for understanding and processing human language, as it helps determine how the meaning of individual sentences combines to convey the overall message of a text. Discourse relations are the fundamental unit of the study of discourse analysis, and they can be broadly categorized into two types: explicit and implicit. Explicit discourse relations are those explicitly marked by discourse connectives, such as “because,” “however,” “therefore,” etc. These connectives provide a direct indication of the relation between the preceding and following clause. On the other hand, implicit discourse relations do not have these explicit linguistic markers.

Social media platforms, such as Twitter and Facebook, are now used by billions of people from all over the world. On these platforms, users communicate and share information in a very informal way using non-standard language. This informal nature of social media text poses a significant challenge for automatic processing of this kind of data because most natural language processing tools expect a formal language input. In recent years, various efforts have been made to develop text preprocessing pipelines for social media text. Among these preprocessing steps, normalization plays a crucial role as it can assist other techniques such as entity recognition, word sense disambiguation and sentiment analysis. For example, it is important to normalize Twitter text "u r funny @mark" to a normalized form "you are funny @mark" to improve the performance of the sentiment analysis task. There have been efforts in recent years to develop text normalization methods suited to the characteristics of social text. Most of these systems derive a comprehensive canonical dictionary by exploiting the "structure" of the informal text. Hence, they are generally termed as dictionary-based approaches. However, these approaches mainly focus on looking for matches in the dictionary and thus lack in the utilization of the contextual and grammatical nuances of social text. For instance, the proposed method will fail to normalize "your funny" in the context "@mark jokes are your funny", as this context requires specific contextual information to determine the correct normalization of "your" as "you're" In this paper, we propose a system for textual normalization designed specifically for the informal nature of social media text. This system is based on graph-based model where words are used as vertices and their contextual and grammatical relationships are considered as edges. We extract two types of features for each vertex: phonetic feature and similarity-based feature. The similarity-based feature is based on both the surface and lexical features of words. The surface similarity feature is calculated using longest common subsequence (LCS) ratio and edit distance measures which are widely used to measure the surface similarity of words (Nagao, 1989;Levenshtein, 1966). The lexical similarity feature is calculated using the matched double metaphone algorithm. We also consider additional contextual information by incorporating part-of-speech (POS) information which is also extracted from the graph. From these features, a word association graph (WAG) is built on which we apply a rank-based method to normalize words.

The key idea of these "zero-shot" approaches is to learn a linear mapping function between two unaligned monolingual vector spaces to induce a bilingual dictionary. The mapping function is typically learned through a translation projection matrix. The most commonly used optimization function for this task is the cross entropy. Results from these papers have shown that zero-shot learning can surprisingly achieve comparable accuracy to that of traditional dictionary alignment methods (e.g., (Schwenk, 2007;Artetxe et al., 2016;Lample and Conneau, 2018;Cer et al., 2018)). Despite these encouraging results, zero-shot learning approaches remain limited in that the learned mappings are not necessarily optimized to produce good translation results on low-resource language pairs, for which the training data is scarce or even non-existent. Moreover, the monolingual word embeddings on which they are built are often obtained from distinct corpora in each language with shallow structures. In this paper, we propose an alternative approach to induce bilingual dictionaries in a more data-driven and interpretative way. Our algorithm builds upon the concept of knowledge distillation. In knowledge distillation, a model (the student) is trained to imitate the outputs of another, learned model (the teacher). Here, we use as teachers rich resource translation paths between languages which are represented as translation contexts. And we use low resource language pairs as learners. The task is to train the learners to imitate the teachers for inducing high-quality bilingual dictionaries. The main contribution of our approach is the design of a knowledge distillation training objective for bilingual dictionary induction. The measured variables for training are translation path confidence scores, which are matched against learned bilingual dictionaries. We design a hierarchical structure for students to learn from teachers. For low resource language pairs, if no teacher exists and there is only one language with a teacher, the learner can learn from the teacher and use its vector as a reference. To enhance vector representations of both the source and target language for better learning, we propose to augment monolingual embeddings with linguistic information. The added information can be morphological or part-of-speech (POS) tags, for example. Both the training objective and the enhanced vector representations contribute to the performance improvement of our technique.

Training neural dialogue systems can be challenging due to the lack of large scale labelled training data and inherent limitations in capturing context. These issues have resulted in subpar performance compared to human generated dialogues when evaluated by humans. Drawing inspiration from the Turing test (Turing 1950)–a test designed to indicate intelligence through indistinguishable responses from a machine – we propose an adversarial learning framework for training neural dialogue generators that maximizes dialogue quality. Our framework is grounded in the intuition that a generated dialogue should closely resemble a human-generated dialogue, as judged by another neural system tasked with discerning human-generated from machine-generated responses. In order to achieve this, we propose an adversarial learning approach where two neural systems, a generator and a discriminator, are jointly trained to augment the dialogue generation problem. The generator outputs a sequence from a discrete space of possible dialogue responses. The discriminator, which we posit to perform as the Turing test evaluator, outputs a binary score indicating the likelihood of the dialogue being human-generated or machine-generated. The discriminator is jointly trained with the generator during the standard process of maximizing the likelihood of human-generated responses and minimizing the likelihood of machine-generated responses. In essence, we train the generator to predict responses that are most likely to fool the discriminator or, conversely, are least likely to be perceived as generated. The discriminator’s output is used as ground truth for training the generator with the objective of fooling the discriminator while the generator attempts to produce responses indistinguishable from human dialogue. We further propose a model for adversarial evaluation, which incorporates the dialogue quality metric directly into the evaluation framework by assessing the likelihood of a dialogue being human-generated. Traditional evaluation measures, such as perplexity or BLEU, do not always reflect dialogue quality from a human perspective. By learning a model that operates on the space of probable dialogues, our approach likely doesn’t learn a simple summary of the data (and the idiosyncrasies of dialogue writing) but instead focuses on generating human-like responses. The model can then be directly evaluated using this adversarial measured, which together with human evaluation can provide more comprehensive quality assessment than traditional metrics alone. We conduct several experiments to test our approach. Our results demonstrate that adversarial learning can indeed train models that generate highly rated responses, as corroborated by both human evaluators and our proposed adversarial metric.

Training discriminative classifiers can be challenging due to the complex internal structures of the training data. We address this challenge in the context of query spelling correction, where the primary goal is to identify the most likely intended query (or "correct" spelling), despite potentially large numbers of candidate corrections obtained from various sources or stages of the correction process, such as token-level n-gram matches or spelling predictions from context (e.g., via Edit Distance, edit-based models, or spell checkers). The training data in such a scenario consists of queries paired with their corrections. The complexity comes from the very large variation in query-correction pairs due to differing typo patterns, word variability (e.g., multiple words with similar phonetics or typing errors), and the need to balance recall (percentage of correct corrections identified) with precision (percentage of identified corrections that are actually correct). The "two-stage" approach as referenced in current methods in query spelling correction (e.g., Bunescu et al., 2007;Wang and Manning, 2010;Jansen and Twidale, 2002) involves a first stage that uses various methods (noise channel models, edit distance-based ranking, etc.) to retrieve a set of candidate corrections for each query, followed by a second stage that discriminatively ranks these candidates and selects the most likely correct correction. The second stage often employs logistic regression, support vector machines (SVM), or other methods that can efficiently handle large candidate sets; however, the performance of these rankers is significantly impacted by the quality of candidates retrieved in the first stage. If the first stage has low recall (i.e., it does not retrieve all or many of the correct corrections in practice), the second stage ranker is faced with a reduced, and potentially suboptimal, set of candidates to rank. This situation can severely limit its effectiveness in identifying the correct correction accurately and lead to a high number of false negatives or poor performance on certain query types. Our approach directly addresses this issue by proposing the use of latent structural SVM (LSSVM) as the discriminative model, which incorporates the structural properties of the data implicitly through a hierarchical structure. Specifically, LSSVM allows us to model the candidate set creation implicitly within the ranking function, rather than relying solely on the first stage to generate candidates. We hypothesized that this might improve performance by allowing the ranking model to better understand the relationships between queries, candidate corrections, and the context of the search query, enabling it to take advantage of potential structural patterns or semantic information within the data even when the first stage's recall is limited.

Tree transducers, which relate tree structures to other tree structures (e.g. first order logic formulas to parse trees or unifier results to DAGs), are useful tools for NLP applications. However, creating a complete, coherent and well-defined grammar for a tree transducer is challenging, time-consuming and often requires expert knowledge. Current research efforts exploit machine learning techniques to automize the grammar induction process (Cohn and Roark, 2010; Li and Hockenmaier, 2010; Schiminovich et al., 2010). However, most of these methods require an additional segmentation step, where input sentences are manually or automatically segmented into bags of word, and assume a probabilistic model for the conditional probability distribution of output trees given the input and the input's features. A different approach, based on matrix factorization derived directly from tree-to-tree pairs (i.e. input sample of size |S| × T , each of size |n| and |m|, respectively), has been used to build string-to-tree transducers (Cohn,2009) and extensions have been explored for similar type transducers (Li and Sun, 2010), but their direct application to tree-to-tree transducers is still lacking. We propose a general algorithm and an exact solution for learning a tree transducer using cost functions defined over tree structures. Unlike traditional machine learning methods, the cost functions directly reflect the syntactic relationships in the trees, and our method does not rely on the availability of feature vectors. As a byproduct of the method, we introduce the concept of "back-off states" which allow the tree transducer learned to generate an output tree even in cases where the correct rule has not yet been shown by the training data. We achieve this by introducing "provisional" costs for unused subtrees in the candidates and the back-off is the implicit use of these costs until a more appropriate rule has been learned. This procedure has been done in Searle's (1970) early work in Machine Translation but never explicitly outlined as a part of the machine learning process. However, it is useful when learning abstract concepts such as verbs acting as predicates in logics, or in our case, generation of sentences from a very changing semantic representation. Our method learns a cost-based tree transducer, where the transducer is conditionally defined on the input tree but also explicitly represented by rules. Our proposed method uses a bottom-up method, initialized by so-called seed rules, which are zero-cost or predefined rules to start with (for example the identity rules).

This allows us to evaluate dialogue in terms of how closely it aligns with or deviates from these normative cooperative behaviors. The goal is not to define non-cooperation as the opposite of cooperation but instead to provide a quantitative measure of how much and in what ways a dialogue deviates from the expected cooperative norms for introducing and discharging conversational obligations. Methodology The proposed method for measuring non-cooperation in dialogue is grounded in the concept of dialogue games, which are derived from a corpus of cooperative dialogues (e.g., interviews, discussions, debates), focusing on specific genres where cooperative norms are expected to be particularly strong (e.g., political interviews, formal debates). The dialogue game is defined through a formalization of the rules that govern "proper" conversation, such as how questions are introduced, candidates are proposed, and obligations are discharged (e.g., through an answer or a relevant follow-up question). The design of these dialogue games is the first step in our method and relies heavily on corpus-based analysis to derive the rules. The model assesses the dialogue in terms of whether it adheres to the conventions provided by the dialogue game. For example, if a dialogue game expects a certain structure for question-answer pairs, the model evaluates if this structure is followed for every question-answer pair in the dialogue.

Automated Essay Scoring (AES) is a critical educative tool that can potentially revolutionize the way teachers assess their students' writing skills. While several AES systems have been developed, they primarily depend on statistical models that are sensitive to the specific writing prompt used to generate the training essays. A particular AES system trained on, for instance, essays written on questions about historical events tends to perform poorly when given essays written on a totally different topic, such as science or literature. The primary reason behind this limitation is the inherent specificity of each writing prompt. A writing prompt not only determines the subject matter of the essay but also influences the choice of verbs, nouns, and even the knowledge domain-specific vocabulary used in the essays. Thus, AES systems trained on essays written in response to one prompt tend to fail when transferred to essays in response to different prompts. This issue is even more pronounced when considering the real-world application of AES systems. The need to grade essays from a wide variety of topics and prompts makes it impractical and cost-prohibitive to manually grade a large number of essays for each new prompt. Obtaining a large corpus of manually graded essays specific to each new prompt is financially and temporally infeasible. Thus, the development of flexible domain adaptation techniques for AES systems is paramount. By enabling AES systems to adapt to new domains (or prompts), we can expand their applicability and reduce the need for human-graded essays specifically for each new domain. ### Flexible Domain Adaptation in Automated Essay Scoring The core challenge in developing domain adaptation for AES lies in finding an effective method to transfer the knowledge from one domain to another without losing the specific prompts' characteristics. This requires not only an understanding of text-based feature representations but also an ability to adapt to domain-specific writing styles and lexical contexts. One promising approach is to model the inter-domain dependencies and learn a mapping between the source and target domains. However, previous domain adaptation techniques have predominantly focused on general cross-domain classification problems and have been less successful in tackling the unique challenges of AES, including the nuanced structure and content dependence of essays. ### Our Proposal: Correlated Linear Regression with Bayesian Regularization We propose a novel domain adaptation method for AES that incorporates correlated linear regression with a Bayesian regularization term. The core idea is to model the dependency structure within and between domains using regression techniques, aiming to capture correlations that span multiple variables and domains.

Named Entity Recognition (NER) is a key component in various Natural Language Processing (NLP) applications. Given a sentence, NER systems aim to identify and categorize names of entities such as people, locations, and organizations. While current NER systems can exhibit good generalization capability and handle unseen entities (entities not present in the training data), accuracy for out-of-domain or unseen entities tends to drop (Asgari et al., 2013). These limitations often come from the inherent reliance of current NER systems on the co-occurrence patterns among word types observed in annotated data. The rarity of out-of-domain entities in training data further deteriorates its model capacity for knowledge generalization. To address this, researchers have tried exploiting extra linguistic knowledge to improve NER systems. Birch and Osborne (2014) used publicly available knowledge to highlight the "spark" relationships among semantic entities. Their model weighted the joint presence of an entity mention with "spark" entities as importance. Asgari and Pilehvar (2015) extended Birch and Osborne's idea and improved NER by explicitly modeling entity-type relationships using typed entity embeddings similar to Collobert and Weston (2008). Recent work by Pilehvar et al. (2017) demonstrated this typed-entity embedding idea further by integrating both entity types and their attributes as multilingual shallow structures. However, these methods still focus on modeling entity co-occurrences in a more structured way and do not provide a principled way to model entity types at a deeper level or to extend easily to new domains or languages. The fundamental task of NER system generalization, especially for out-of-domain or new entities, remains as a challenge. One potential key is the exploitation of a large, multilingual and "universal" knowledge graph like Wikipedia, which contains millions of entities and their structured descriptions. Wikipedia's entity types (e.g., "Location", "Person") and attributes (e.g., "Birthdate", "Location") could provide the necessary knowledge for a better understanding of entity semantics, benefiting the generalization of NER systems. However, directly using Wikipedia data is challenging because it contains rich unstructured information that is less suitable for direct usage in statistical NLP models. Moreover, changing domains or languages in Wikipedia calls for new entity type mappings, which is non-trivial because of cross-lingual and cross-domain discrepancies. In this paper, we propose a new method for improving multilingual NER by leveraging Wikipedia for information about entity types and their mappings to labels in the training set.

Automatic keyphrase generation (KFG) is a fundamental task of text summarization and document-level information retrieval (DIIR). Automatic keyphrase generation aims to select a set of keyphrases (or keywords) that are well-representative of a given document, and indispensable for tasks like document summarization (Hovy and Slutsky, 2008;Ratinov and Roth, 2009), web-page access (Pang and Lee, 2004), academic search (Reynaert et al., 2011), and query refinement (Evans and al., 1993;Song et al., 2007). Despite its importance, there have been few attempts at studying the correlation among keyphrases. The lack of correlation analysis may lead to duplication or coverage issues, as multiple keyphrases can indicate the same meaning or concept in a document. For example, in the source document "For batteries that power everything from electric vehicles to data centers, its supply chains are vital", automatic keyphrase generation systems may output both "electric vehicle" and "vehicles", resulting in duplications. Furthermore, the correlation among keyphrases may not be fully exploited or even ignored. For instance, a keyphrase like "batteries", which conceptually relates to "electric vehicle", might not appear in the final keyphrase set if assumed to be the 'main' object. The problem of identifying and modeling the correlations between keyphrases can serve multiple purposes. On the one hand, handling correlations can improve the accuracy of the generated keyphrases by avoiding duplications and ensuring coverage of different aspects in the document. For example, keyphrases "software", "engineering", and "technology" can all relate to "science and technology", but each subsumes different aspects of the broader topic. On the other hand, understanding the correlations among keyphrases can enhance the interpretability and coherence of the generated keyphrases, which are desirable properties for real-world applications. To address these challenges, we propose a novel approach to automatically generate keyphrases that can capture correlations among candidate phrases. Specifically, we argue that a systematic understanding of concepts and their changing relationships across texts can help generate more accurate, comprehensive, and coherent keyphrases. Our approach is grounded in the observation that in natural language, several keyphrases often express different facets or perspectives of the same concept or semantic cluster within a document. For example, in an essay discussing the benefits of renewable energy sources, the keyphrases "solar", "hydroelectric", and "wind energy" all reflect different types of renewable energy, thus conceptually connected. Our task is to generate keyphrases that capture these connections and variations, while avoiding duplication and ensuring all relevant aspects of the document content are represented.

Certainly, here is my answer: Graphical models over strings offer a powerful framework for capturing complex patterns in character or word-level data. Such models can represent dependencies and interactions between different components of strings, such as characters within words, words within sentences, or even sentences within discourses. Expectation Propagation (EP) (Minka, 2001) is an efficient algorithm for approximate inference in these graphical models. It iteratively adjusts messages between "nodes" in the graph to approximate inference, often with higher accuracy than loopy belief propagation (LoopyBP), and it can handle complex data dependencies that keeps it backwards compatible with probabilistic graphical models over latent variables (Gilks and Wild, 1992). EP is particularly useful for tasks such as sequence analysis, alignment, and language modeling, where strings are of interest, but its downside is that inference can be computationally costly for large datasets or complex dependency structures. In such situations, making approximations on the form of the messages can help. Recent work has explored approximations such as variational approximations (e.g., Lee et al., 2015) or the ensembling of belief functions (Zanfir et al., 2014) to speed up inference, while others have proposed simplifying the message passing itself (Moo et al., 2016). A balance between accuracy and computational efficiency in message passing is difficult because the simplest assumed message typically comes from an empirical distribution over the data, but this often overfits and ignores useful model regularization or prior knowledge. A key insight in solving this trade-off for graphical models over strings is structured sparsity. A structured sparsity penalty encourages certain patterns in the model parameters in accordance with domain-specific constraints. One such domain is the representation of strings, which are naturally amenable to "sparse" representations using models such as n-grams (Baayen, 2001) which represent strings as the combination of local patterns of high-order context (such as bigrams, trigrams, etc). More specifically, in the context of probabilistic graphical models over strings, a penalization encouraging sparse patterns in the approximate distribution over strings can be explicitly tied to storing low-order n-grams for each node in the graph, but also implicitly tied to higher-order dependencies across longer dependency structures within the graph (e.g., modeling a word by its characters but also aggregating some influence from larger substrings/predictors like prefixes or suffixes when relevant). In this paper, we introduce Penalized Expectation Propagation (PEP), a novel algorithm for approximate inference in graphical models.

Training embeddings using large unlabelled text corpora with unsupervised methods such as Word2Vec (Mikolov et al., 2013) or GloVe (Pennington et al., 2014) has become a powerful way to represent words or other textual elements as vectors, capturing a kind of "meaning" or "similarity" between words or texts (Pennington, Socher, & Manning, 2014). The representation has shown to capture various types of analogical relationships among word pairs (Mikolov et al., 2013). This representation has been successfully integrated into many NLP systems to achieve state-of-the-art results in tasks such as question answering (Hu et al., 2014), sentence embedding similarity prediction (Søgaard and Goldberg, 2016), and named-entity recognition (Bansal et al., 2014). However, while unsupervised embedding approaches can capture semantic relationships among words, they are limited in that they do not explicitly capture how words in a sentence compose their meaning and build up abstract representations. To address this limitation, recent studies have explored the sequential structure of sentences and demonstrated that learning representations based on word sequences within sentences can more accurately capture sentence meanings (Socher et al., 2011; Le and Mikolov, 2014; Kiros et al., 2015). Such models learn representations at the sentence or document level by processing individual words in context through sequential models such as recurrent neural networks (RNNs) (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997) or by encoding words into vectors based on the words and their contexts using attention mechanisms and encoder-decoder RNNs (Sutskever et al., 2014; Bahdanau et al., 2015; Vaswani et al., 2017; Gehring et al., 2018). To apply deep models for question answering or other downstream tasks that require detailed comprehension of sentences, we need sentence-level representations that accurately capture the meaning of sentences. While various methods (Socher et al., 2011; Le and Mikolov, 2014; Kiros et al., 2015) can generate sentence-level representations and achieve promising results on certain tasks, they suffer from different limitations. These include zero shot performance: these models are not designed to handle the case where the training data does not have overlapping words with the testing data; robustness to noise in the training set; ability to generalize to unseen sentences and contexts, including examples that are syntactically and conceptually different from any training instances; trade-offs between computational complexity and memory constraints during training and inference (especially for large models and long sentences); and difficulty in dealing with open domain text that encompasses a wide range of topics and rare words.

Readability of text is a crucial factor in communication, affecting both educative and social contexts. Computational approaches to measuring readability can automate this process and assist in analyzing and improving the readability of texts. However, readability is not a fixed property of text but can vary depending on the background and expertise of the target reader, as well as the properties of the text itself. In this paper, we present an investigation into the interplay between reader background and text features in determining readability in Bangla, a language which has not benefited from extensive readability studies as have other major languages such as English. We set out to create a novel Bangla readability dataset, alongside a set of features that characterizes the texts and measures the reading difficulty, as perceived by readers. ### 1. Introduction Readability is defined as the ease with which a reader can comprehend a text (Guthrie et al., 2004). Texts of varying readability can affect the effectiveness of communication, particularly in education where learning outcomes are closely linked to the ease with which students can understand assigned materials (Chall, 1996). In Bangla, the official language of Bangladesh and a major spoken language in India, text readability has not received the attention seen in other linguistic environments, such as English. Our work seeks to address this gap. ### 2. Dataset Creation Our dataset is composed of 135 documents, each annotated by 50 readers from two different backgrounds. The readers are categorized into two groups: 25 general readers (with no special expertise or knowledge in a particular domain or subject area) and 25 specialists (with undergraduate or higher education in a particular subject area relevant to the texts). Each text is annotated by both group members based on a readability scale. ### 3. Text and Reader Features To model perceived ease of readability, we identified 20 features that are potentially relevant in Bangla texts. The features were broadly categorized into two groups: #### 3.1 Classic Features: - Character count per word. - Word count per sentence. - Sentence length. - Number of complex/compounded words. - Number of abstract concepts. - Use of technical vocabulary. - Diversity of vocabulary (type-token ratio). - Frequency of rare/archaic words. #### 3.2 Non-Classic Features: - Proportion of contractions/shortened forms in dialogue/personal writings. - Use of punctuation marks. - Proportion of direct speech over narrative. - Average length of nominal phrases. - Proportion of active versus passive voice use. - Average complexity of sentence structure as measured by dependency length.

However, these models can still suffer from interference when they share too much information between the different tasks, or use unrelated resources for the wrong tasks. Most existing neural multi-task learning methods apply one–or-a-variable number of network layers to all tasks, without any mechanism to filter or modify the information being shared (Cui et al., 2017). This "one-size-fits-all" design leads to inefficient and possibly harmful information exchange among tasks. Table 1 (left) outlines a number of existing methods that keeps changing network weights alongside with fine-tuned task-specific sub-network training. At first glance, a solution for this issue would seem to be to just keep these weights fixed, or only fine tune a certain selection of them (as commonly applies to transfer learning among semantic tasks (Long et al., 2014;Donahue et al., 2014;Torrey et al., 2010)). However, completely preventing communication between tasks makes it difficult to explore the potential benefits of shared knowledge. Our proposed method is a deep hierarchical network that introduces a novel share-and-select mechanism at the layer level or even at the unit level For each task, this mechanism operates on the output from the shared units and selectively passes information between different tasks based on the task identities and their corresponding assumed shared features. We call this mechanism "Leaky Units" as a metaphor for forgetting irrelevant or conflicting information while retaining the useful knowledge. We first design an inference graph (Figure 1), which separates task specific heads from the shared, learned knowledge. Each task head can in principle be as simple as a classifier stacked on top of the shared feature map. Each memory holds the value of the unit measured in relation to the specific task and the overall shared layer. The base of the unit keeps updating whenever it is activated, allowing for recent events or tasks to be memorized more strongly . Meanwhile, an additional forget gate controls how much previous task changing the value of shared memory. This is done using a parameterized leaky factor, which can make the current value for a particular task depend not only on what it currently sees, but also what it has seen previously for different tasks(Figure 2).

These SCFGs have faster decoding times but can be limited in the linguistic phenomena that they can properly model. On the other hand, SCFGs with higher inference complexity (typically cubic in terms of the size of the input) necessitate a more elegant approach to ensure efficient decoding. Since SCFGs in Chomsky Normal Form (CNF) support cubic or better time polynomial-time decoding For a survey of this, refer to (DeNero and Klein, 2009). the practice has been to perform synchronous binarization (Zhang et al., 2006; Zollmann et al., 2011), a technique that rewrites the grammar into an equivalent CNF grammar while preserving inference complexity. Although synchronous binarization ensures efficient decoding, it is known to introduce in practice a higher constant factor (DeNero et al., 2009). In fact, (DeNero et al., 2009) have identified and quantified how this constant factor can influence the practical performance of SCFG decoders, particularly when coupled with heuristic search algorithms. Their work showed that the binarization step contributes significantly to the real-world efficiency of the decoding algorithm. Several approaches were proposed to mitigate this issue. For example, storing binarized grammars for repeated use in closed vocabulary scenarios (Zhang et al., 2006). Semantic relatedness measures typically aim to quantify the degree to which two terms or words are conceptually related. For instance, this could apply to synonymy, hyponymy, antonymy, or even hypernymy relations. The assumed hypothesis is that terms that are semantically related in a way relevant to the IR task (such as the core concepts of a query matching key terms in retrieved documents) will increase the likelihood of relevance. The fundamental task, therefore, is to accurately identify such semantic relatedness between terms in user queries and those within documents in an IR corpus. From early works like Wilensky’s and Hirschfeld’s (1992) semantic relatedness measure, which used distributional and the Boolean analysis of subject-verb-object collocations, to more recent and sophisticated approaches such as WordNet (Miller, 1995), measured through synonymy-based metrics or dependence syntax, various methods have been developed.
